docs.title: When something will not go through
When something will not go through
docs.text: The situations you actually meet, with their cause and what to do. Almost all of them have the same origin: a condition set upstream is not met, and the screen refuses rather than guesses.

docs.title: "I see no campaign"
docs.text:
Three possible causes, in order of frequency.

The campaign is not open. Only the Opened state accepts wishes. A "Ready" campaign is visible to you, not to your students.

The student is not in the pool. The campaign's criteria — level, track, campus, tags, filters — do not retain them. Open the campaign and look at the list of participants: if they are not there, add them by hand.

The student has no profile. With no file, they exist for no campaign.

docs.title: "I cannot submit my wishes"
docs.text: You set a minimum number of wishes and they have not reached it. The minimum blocks just as the maximum does.

docs.title: "I find no destination"
docs.text:
The campaign's destination pool is empty, or no place is set on the agreements it retains. Check the place matrix before looking elsewhere: a destination with no place does not show.

Check the period too: a place always exists for a given period.

docs.title: "I no longer see my ranking"
docs.text: That is deliberate, if your institution hid the ranking from students. The setting is in What your students see — you and your team still see it.

docs.title: "I did not get my access"
docs.text: An access opened is not an access received. Look at the access state column on your student list: it says whether it left and when. And the Connected column says whether they have signed in — these are two different questions.

docs.title: "The matching round refuses to start"
docs.text:
This is the most frequent block, and it is always explained: the report names the students standing in the way, and why.

Message What to do The student has no track Attach them to one. If your institution uses none, create one per level. The student has no ranking Import the ranking before re-running. The round does not produce one. The student has no profile There is nothing to place. Their file is incomplete Complete it, or set the campaign to "flag" rather than "block".

The round is not a one-shot

Fix what blocks and run it again, as often as needed.

docs.title: "I cannot delete this campaign"
docs.text: Only a draft campaign can be deleted. An open campaign already carries wishes.

docs.title: "I cannot reopen this campaign"
docs.text: Only a finished campaign can be reopened. And if you reopen it without pushing its end date back, it will close again the next morning.

docs.title: "My campaign closed by itself"
docs.text: Its end date has passed. That is normal behaviour since September 2026: the morning after the last day, the campaign closes, draft wishes become wishes and you receive the summary. Reopen it and push the date back if that was premature.

docs.title: "My place counters disagree with my export"
docs.text: Since September 2026, every place counter covers outgoing mobilities only — the ones you send. Places your partners open at home no longer inflate your totals. If a figure surprises you, it was most likely wrong before.

docs.title: "I cannot remind this partner"
docs.text: One reminder per twenty-four hours. The button greys out afterwards, and tells you when.

docs.title: "I cannot nominate this student on this agreement"
docs.text: A nomination is already live on that agreement for them. Withdraw it first if you want to start again.

docs.title: "This partner does not appear in my campaign"
docs.text: The destination pool does not retain it: check the campaign's agreement types, periods and institution filters. Check too that it is not archived or hidden.

docs.title: "I cannot refuse this nomination"
docs.text: A refusal asks for a reason. It will be passed on to the institution that nominated the student to you.

docs.title: "This screen is read-only"
docs.text: Your role gives you the View level on this section. A banner says so at the top of the screen. Your My permissions screen tells you exactly what you can do, and to whom.

docs.title: "This student is outside my perimeter"
docs.text: Your role is limited to a direction, a campus or cohorts that do not cover them. This is not a breakdown: it is the perimeter your administrator defined.

docs.title: "Part of my selection was not processed"
docs.text: Your action covered rows outside your perimeter. They are set aside, and the screen tells you which.

docs.title: "I cannot sign in with my institution account"
docs.text: Single sign-on verifies who you are; it does not decide that you are allowed in. Your account must already exist in AroundLink. See Who provides what.

docs.title: "I cannot save this language score"
docs.text: A score always needs supporting evidence. The file and the date are required.

docs.title: "I am asked for a reason to change the learning agreement"
docs.text: Any component added or removed after validation asks for a justification. That is a requirement of the agreement, not a setting.

docs.title: AroundLink product documentation
docs.text:
AroundLink is the international student mobility platform (Erasmus+ / EWP) used by the International Relations (IRO) offices of higher-education institutions. It brings partners, agreements, application campaigns, contractual documents, grants and data exchange with the European network into one place — replacing scattered spreadsheets and emails with a single, auditable, compliant process.

This documentation lists every feature of the tool and, for each one, its business value. It serves you:

  • International-office managers and officers: understand what the tool does and the value it brings, without technical jargon.
  • IT departments: the Platform pages answer questions on connection, authentication and data exchange.

How to read a feature card

Every feature follows the same format: what it is for, who it is for, how it works, and a concrete use case. Call-outs flag what you should know before turning a setting on, and the traps you only see once you are in.

Useful addresses

The application: app.aroundlink.com — where you work day to day.

The AroundLink website: aroundlink.com — the product presentation, and how to reach us.

A meeting: thirty minutes with our team — to talk about your own institution rather than hunting for the answer page by page.

This documentation describes what the tool does; it does not replace the application.

docs.title: The three spaces
docs.text:
• Institution workspace

    The IRO team's workspace: agenda, partners and agreements, campaigns, mobility paths and tracking, incoming students, documents, grants, communications and steering.

    Dashboard

  • Student portal

    The student journey, from discovering destinations to applying, then during and after the mobility (learning agreement, certificates, transcript of records).

    Discover & apply

  • Atlas & EWP network

    The world directory of institutions and the integration with the Erasmus Without Paper network to exchange agreements, learning agreements and transcripts without paper.

    Atlas · EWP

docs.title: A word on multi-tenancy
docs.text: AroundLink is a multi-tenant SaaS platform: each client institution only ever sees its own data (students, agreements, campaigns…), fully isolated from every other institution. Three account types coexist — IRO coordinator, student and invited partner — each with its own space and permissions. See Platform & security.

docs.title: A mobility from end to end
A mobility from end to end
docs.text:
This page follows one whole mobility, from the first setting to the transcript, saying at each step who acts and what triggers the next one.

The rest of the documentation describes screens one by one. This one describes the sequence — which is often what is missing when you are looking for why a file is not moving.

docs.title: Before any campaign: the groundwork
docs.text:
Nothing below works if these four things do not exist.

What you need Who prepares it Without it Your partners and their agreements Coordinator No destination to offer Places set in the matrix Coordinator Destinations exist but open nothing Your tracks (one per cohort, or one per level) Administrator, in settings The matching round refuses to start Your mobility periods Administrator Places have no column to sit in

The most common false start

Creating a campaign before setting any places. The campaign opens, students see it, and find no destination. Check the matrix before you open.

docs.title: 1. The campaign opens
docs.text:
Who acts: the coordinator.

They create the campaign, choose who takes part and where one can go, set the number of wishes, the required documents and the few options that cannot be revisited later. See Setting up a campaign, setting by setting.

The campaign moves from Draft to Ready, then Opened.

What triggers the next step: only the Opened state accepts wishes. A "Ready" campaign can be looked at, not filled in.

docs.title: 2. The student places their wishes
docs.text:
Who acts: the student.

They browse destinations, set some aside as favourites, and place their wishes from the very screen where they discover them. They rank them by preference.

If you set a minimum number of wishes, they cannot submit until they reach it. If you enabled the "I do not wish to go" answer, they can also declare it — without having to justify themselves.

What triggers the next step: the campaign closing, on its end date or by your hand. Wishes still in draft then become real wishes.

docs.title: 3. Placement
docs.text:
Who acts: the coordinator.

Two paths, which coexist.

The automatic round serves students in ranking order: the first-ranked gets their best available wish, and what is left goes to the next. It requires a profile, a track and an imported ranking from every participant — see What matching requires. It can be re-run as often as needed.

Placing by hand is constrained by nothing. You seat whoever you want, wherever you want, ranked or not.

What triggers the next step: a placement exists.

docs.title: 4. The student accepts — or not
docs.text:
Who acts: the student, unless you chose direct assignment.

They receive their proposal and accept or decline it. If you set the campaign to direct assignment, this step disappears: your decision creates the placement.

What triggers the next step: acceptance.

docs.title: 5. Nominating to the partner
docs.text:
Who acts: the coordinator, then the host institution.

You nominate the student to their destination. The partner receives the information and answers — through the platform, the EWP network, email or a phone call. You record their answer, stating which channel it came through.

While they have not answered, you can remind them (once every twenty-four hours) or withdraw the nomination, which makes the student available for another destination.

A refusal always comes with a reason, passed on to the institution that nominated.

What triggers the next step: the partner's confirmation.

docs.title: 6. The file fills up
docs.text:
Who acts: the student uploads, the coordinator validates.

Contractual documents, language scores, learning agreement. Every expected item is listed, and the student sees what is missing. You remind the stragglers from the selection bar of your list, without keeping a separate list.

Depending on the campaign setting, an incomplete file either blocks the placement or is merely flagged.

What triggers the next step: the file is complete, and the dates are near.

docs.title: 7. Departure, then the stay
docs.text:
Who acts: everyone, a little at a time.

The student leaves. Their learning agreement can be changed along the way — any component change asks for a reason. The period's deadlines appear in the agenda, and in whichever calendar each person subscribed to.

docs.title: 8. Coming back
docs.text:
Who acts: the host institution, then the student.

The institution that hosted enters the grades in its own scale and issues the transcript; the student is notified and finds it on their file.

The student submits their feedback on the host institution — and may allow their photos to be published. Those who have not answered are reminded like documents.

What closes the loop: feedback feeds the partner's record, which the next students will read before placing their wishes.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The acronyms and terms you meet across AroundLink and international mobility.

Term Definition IR office The international relations office of a school or university — the team this documentation is written for. IRO International Relations Office — the team that manages mobility at an institution. DRI / Head of IR The strategic steering of international mobility. Erasmus+ The European Union's mobility programme, which funds student exchanges among other things. EWP Erasmus Without Paper — the European network for digital exchange of mobility data between institutions. See EWP network. IIA Inter-Institutional Agreement — the Erasmus+ agreement signed between two universities. Bilateral agreement A direct cooperation agreement (outside Erasmus/EWP) negotiated between two institutions. Double degree A joint programme where the student earns a degree at both institutions. Paying mobility A study abroad mobility where the student pays fees to the host institution. OLA Online Learning Agreement — the digital learning agreement: the list of courses taken abroad and their recognition. Learning Agreement The learning agreement (see OLA). ToR Transcript of Records — the official transcript of the mobility. ECTS European Credit Transfer System — the European credit system (30 ECTS ≈ one semester). Factsheet An institution's practical fact sheet (deadlines, housing/visa contacts…), exchanged over EWP. Nomination The official proposal of a student to a host institution, which accepts or rejects it. Affectation / placement A student's confirmed placement on a destination, within a campaign. Wish A destination choice ranked by the student during a campaign. Campaign A framed application round (dates, levels, number of wishes) run by the IRO. Place distribution The breakdown of an agreement's places by year, level, period and field. CNR Change Notification Receiver — the EWP notification telling a partner that data changed. HEI Higher Education Institution; the HEI ID is its EWP identifier. SCHAC A standard institution identifier (based on its domain). Erasmus code An institution's official Erasmus code. ROR Research Organization Registry — a global open registry of research/education organisations, the basis of Atlas. ECHE Erasmus Charter for Higher Education — the charter that accredits an institution for the programme. EQF European Qualifications Framework — the European framework of qualification levels (e.g. EQF 6 = bachelor, 7 = master, 8 = doctorate). ISCED The international classification of fields of education (discipline). OUnit Organizational Unit — a faculty/department of an institution, in the EWP sense. Mobility grant The Erasmus+ financial support paid to the student. See Mobility grants. Beneficiary Module The official Erasmus+ tool where an institution reports its mobilities. SSO Single Sign-On — signing in with an existing account (e.g. Microsoft/Azure). Multi-tenant (SaaS) The architecture where each client institution is isolated from others on a shared platform.

docs.title: Words that get confused
docs.text: Eight pairs of terms that look alike and do not mean the same thing. They are by far the first source of misunderstanding between a team and its tool.

docs.title: Wish, proposal, placement, nomination
docs.text:
Four words for four distinct moments of the same file, in this order:

Term Who issues it What it is Wish The student A destination they ask for, ranked by preference Proposal The tool or the coordinator A destination offered to them, which they can still decline Placement The coordinator, or the student's acceptance The destination retained — the file has a seat Nomination The coordinator, towards the partner The official announcement to the host institution

A student may have five wishes, one proposal, one placement and one nomination. It is not the same thing in four places: it is four steps.

docs.title: Academic level and track
docs.text:
The academic level is a shared European scale — bachelor, master, doctorate. It lets you compare two students from two countries.

The track is the label you give your cohorts: "Aero 4", "MSc 26-27". It only means something at home, and it is what designates the cell in the place matrix.

That is why the matching round requires a track and not just a level: "Aero 4" and "Aero 5" are both master's, and do not open the same places.

docs.title: Tag and student filter
docs.text: A tag stays with you. A student filter can be shown to your students, who use it to search for a destination. See Tag or student filter?.

docs.title: Agreement, exchange, place
docs.text:
The agreement is the contract binding you to a partner — it has a type, dates, signatories.

The exchange is a line of that agreement: a direction, a level, a field.

The place is an available seat, for a given period and track. It is what the student occupies. An agreement can exist without opening a single place.

docs.title: Outgoing and incoming
docs.text:
Outgoing: your students leaving. Incoming: the students you host.

Since September 2026, every place counter covers outgoing only. An agreement often opens places both ways; only those you send count towards your totals.

docs.title: Ready and Opened
docs.text: A Ready campaign is visible to your team, and to them alone. An Opened campaign is where your students place their wishes. This confusion explains most of the "my students see nothing".

docs.title: Access opened and account connected
docs.text: Access opened: you sent their invitation. Connected: they used it. Two separate columns, because they call for two different reminders.

docs.title: Client partner and non-client partner
docs.text:
A partner that uses AroundLink itself publishes its information: its factsheet, course catalogue, library, FAQ. You read them as they write them, and they update by themselves.

A partner that does not use it publishes nothing. What you write about them is then yours, and your institution alone sees it.

docs.title: Atlas — World directory
docs.text: Atlas is a worldwide directory of higher-education institutions: a single place to search for any institution, locate it on a world map, and immediately see whether it is already a partner or reachable through the Erasmus/EWP network. "Who else is out there?" becomes a map you explore, rather than a spreadsheet.

docs.title: World directory (table / cards / map)
docs.text:
What it's for. Atlas gathers every higher-education institution in the world into a searchable directory. You look up any institution, see where it sits on a map, and tell at a glance which ones are already your partners from those reachable through the EWP network.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. A single page offers three synchronized views: table, cards and an interactive world map. You filter by free text (name, city), country, institution type and EWP factsheet status. Each row shows its network status and marks the institutions already partnered with your institution. The page is read-only: you consult it, you don't create or edit a record here.

Atlas in map view: each dot is an institution from the world registry. The Table and Cards views offer the same search.

Use case.

A coordinator searches "Antalya", filters to Turkey, sees on the map which nearby universities already expose an EWP factsheet, and spots that one of them is already a partner.

The same search in cards view: each institution with its country, its type and whether it is connected to the EWP network.

docs.title: Live factsheet on demand
docs.text:
What it's for. From any institution in the network, you open its EWP factsheet live — nomination deadlines, application contacts — without waiting for a bulk sync. The directory fills in over time as institutions are consulted.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. Opening an institution's record fetches its factsheet live (if declared), then shows the nomination calendar (autumn / spring) and application contact details (email, phone). A successful lookup updates the institution's cached summary, so the directory fills in as it is used.

Use case.

Before nominating their students, a coordinator opens a partner's factsheet to confirm the spring nomination deadline.

docs.title: Agreements & place distribution
docs.text: The Agreements module brings together everything an institution can offer its students: Erasmus+/IIA exchanges, non-network bilateral agreements, double degrees and paying mobilities. Every agreement carries its places, finely distributed by year, level, period and field, feeding directly into the catalogue students see.

docs.title: Exchange offers (inter-institutional agreements / IIA)
docs.text:
What it's for. This is the reference catalogue of the mobilities a student can apply to: an exchange signed with a partner institution, describing academic levels, languages, subject areas (ISCED), requirements and the number of places. The same record doubles as the Erasmus+/IIA file, so the information is never managed twice.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator creates or imports an exchange, then attaches one or more mobility blocks (studies, traineeship, staff), each specifying the expected languages, subject areas, requirements and a place allotment. Dedicated pages let you view the information, conditions, approval status and history, sync the EWP factsheet and notify the partner. A student's eligibility (level, period, GPA, language scores) is checked automatically at application time.

All your agreements across every partner: type, status, levels, languages, validity and places. Click the image to enlarge it.

Use case.

The IRO records an Erasmus+ exchange with TU Munich: 3 Master places in engineering, English B2 required, IIA identifier synced with the partner over EWP.

docs.title: Place distribution (allocation matrix)
docs.text:
What it's for. Rather than a single overall number, the institution spreads its negotiated places across a precise grid: academic year, academic level, mobility period and subject area (ISCED). This distribution feeds the places table shown to students and enforces each agreement's annual cap.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. On an exchange's place-distribution page, the coordinator fills in a matrix (year × field × level × period). The system checks each mobility block's annual cap before saving, updates the affected cells and groups levels by EQF framework so related programmes stay together. The result is immediately visible to students.

The allocation grid: academic years split by period across the columns, your study levels grouped by European framework down the rows. The summary at the bottom flags an overrun of the negotiated annual cap in red.

Use case.

A partner grants 4 places: the office assigns 2 to Master / Semester 1 and 2 to Master / Semester 2 for 2026/2027; the student sees exactly that breakdown on the partner's page.

docs.title: Staff places are not distributed
docs.text:
Why. The matrix is a study level × period grid. A teacher belongs to no intake: no cell can hold them. The grid was therefore filled in by default, for want of saying it served no purpose.

How it works. An agreement carrying only staff mobility no longer shows a matrix, and the screen explains why. An agreement with no conditions at all keeps its own: the boundary is "there are conditions, but none for students".

The negotiated envelope stays readable. It is genuine agreement data, negotiated per audience, and the Agreements and Institutions grids now show it in three columns where a single one used to add them up:

Column What it counts students studies and traineeship together — one audience from the coordinator's point of view teachers teaching mobility staff staff training

A dash, not a zero, when there is no agreement for that audience: a zero would read as an envelope negotiated down to zero.

Two neighbouring figures, two meanings

These three columns say what was signed. The Places / year column next to them counts what was distributed in the matrices. An agreement could show 28 places, 24 of them staff training, with nothing saying so.

docs.title: A place carries the location it is meant for
docs.text:
How it works. A place belongs to its agreement and names the location where the student is expected. When a partner has several cities, those cities' matrices stack up in the same page, each announcing what it already carries — the institution itself counts among the locations, labelled Main.

Three campuses therefore do not add three agreements, and a terminated agreement stops distributing its places, whatever its family.

docs.title: A unified places engine
docs.text:
What it's for. Every agreement type — exchange, bilateral, double degree, paying mobility — presents its places to students and to the administration in the same way. The catalogue stays consistent whatever the underlying contract type.

Who it's for. admin

How it works. Each agreement type exposes its places in a common form, grouped by mobility category (Exchange, Double Degree, Internship, Paying mobility) then by field, year, level and period. The same construction feeds the student page and the coordinator preview, which therefore always stay in sync.

Use case.

A partner offers both an Erasmus exchange and a double degree: the student sees two category tabs, each with its own places grid.

docs.title: Bilateral agreements
docs.text:
What it's for. Manages non-Erasmus partnerships built on a genuine negotiation between two institutions — one owner (paying offer), one partner (free offer) — with their own place distribution. Covers cooperation outside the EWP/Erasmus network.

Who it's for. IRO manager / partner

How it works. The owning institution drafts an agreement, then submits it; the partner reviews, approves or modifies it. Any edit by either side restarts the cycle until both approvals line up: the agreement then becomes active. A place-distribution matrix is filled in for student mobilities. An import with preview is available.

Use case.

A French school signs a bilateral exchange with a Brazilian partner outside Erasmus; both coordinators approve in the tool, then the French side distributes 2 Master places in Semester 1.

docs.title: Double degrees
docs.text:
What it's for. Manages double-degree partnerships, where a student earns a degree at both institutions over several years: yearly phases, joint curriculum, graduation conditions and common jury. A different framework from a simple exchange.

Who it's for. IRO manager / partner

How it works. Same two-sided negotiation as bilateral agreements (drafting, submission, approval), with an invitation sent to the partner signatory at submission. The agreement carries curriculum, graduation, jury, EQF level and duration information, plus yearly phases (Year 1 / Year 2). Places are distributed via a dedicated matrix. An import with preview is available.

Use case.

A Master double degree with Georgia Tech over 2 years: the student goes abroad in year 2; the office tracks each phase and distributes the yearly places.

docs.title: Paying mobility (study abroad)
docs.text:
What it's for. Manages fee-based "study abroad" placements, where the student pays tuition to the host institution and the home institution owns the agreement end to end. Distinguishes fee-generating mobility from free Erasmus exchange.

Who it's for. IRO manager (creation) · student (viewing the price)

How it works. The coordinator drafts then publishes the agreement (a single owner, with no two-sided negotiation phase): fee amount, currency, subtype (individual placement or high volume), duration and mobility type. They then distribute places via the distribution matrix. When an institution offers paying mobility, these offers are visible to students (in "Find Exchange") with their indicative price, so the student knows the cost before applying. An import with preview is available.

Use case.

A partner in the US where the student pays $12,000 in tuition: the office records it as a "study abroad" paying agreement and publishes 5 places for the year.

docs.title: Proof of an agreement's conditions
docs.text:
What it's for. Keep, on the agreement itself, the documents evidencing its conditions: the signed convention, an amendment, an exchange of letters, a fee schedule.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. Each agreement — bilateral, double degree or paying mobility — has an upload area on its conditions screen. Documents stay attached to the agreement, separate from student files, and remain readable even once the agreement expires.

Use case.

The coordinator uploads the signed convention to the double-degree agreement; two years later their successor finds it without digging through the office archives.

docs.title: Agreement CSV imports
docs.text:
What it's for. Lets you load agreements in bulk from a spreadsheet rather than one by one, with a preview-and-correct step before validation to catch bad rows. Speeds up onboarding of large partner portfolios.

Who it's for. IRO manager

How it works. Each agreement family (exchanges, IIA, bilateral, double degree, paying) has its own import page. The file is first parsed and checked row by row in a preview, where each row can be corrected, before a final validation that saves everything. File templates are downloadable.

Use case.

An office pastes 80 exchanges from a legacy spreadsheet, fixes 3 flagged rows in the preview, then validates.

docs.title: Agreement update review (IIA)
docs.text:
What it does. When a partner institution pushes changes to an inter-institutional agreement (IIA) over the EWP network, this review shows a field-by-field comparison and lets you selectively accept or reject the changes before they touch local data.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator opens the pending update and sees the comparison between their version and the partner's. They tick the fields to accept and apply — a count of applied/skipped fields is shown — or reject the update, in which case their data stays unchanged.

Use case.

The partner changes the agreement's ECTS and languages; the coordinator accepts the language change but rejects the ECTS one — only the accepted field is written locally.

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text:
The agenda brings every date of your institution into one place: semesters, campaigns, your partners' deadlines, onboarding steps, nominations and events.

These dates used to live in five different screens, and nobody could simply answer "what is due next month?".

docs.title: What you find there
docs.text:
What it's for. Seeing what is coming. A nomination deadline, a campaign closing and a partner's term start are not the same kind of thing, but they fall in the same month, and that is what matters when you organise your work.

Who it's for. the whole mobility team

How it works. The agenda invents no date and changes none: it assembles what already exists elsewhere. Each entry links back to the object it comes from, and that is where the date is edited — otherwise two versions of the same deadline would end up contradicting each other.

The agenda opens on the month grid. You switch to a list view when you would rather read everything in a row, and you filter on:

  • the family — Semesters, Campaigns, Partners, Nomination, Onboarding, Application, Other;
  • the direction — outgoing or incoming;
  • your team only, to set aside what does not concern you.

Filters stack, and the filter bar stays in view as the list scrolls.

You can also add a date by hand, for what exists nowhere else: a committee meeting, an internal deadline.

On the student side, the agenda is the timeline of their mobility. Their campaign dates and their path dates come together there, sorted into overdue, upcoming and past. The current day does not count as past, and a campaign date appears even if the student has submitted no wish.

The current month, each date carrying its family's colour. At the top, the filters that stack and the button to subscribe from your own calendar.

docs.title: Collecting your partners' dates
docs.text:
What it is for. You cannot keep sixty universities' calendars up to date. They can — each their own. The agenda lets you ask them.

Who it is for. IO officer / coordinator

How it works. You ask for the deadlines of one partner, or of all of them in one gesture. They receive a link that needs no account: they fill in their dates, which come back into your agenda, attached to them. The form carries your logo, so they know who is asking.

You are told as soon as a partner has answered: a notification arrives in the tool, you have nothing to watch.

Six kinds of date are collected this way:

What you ask for For which intake Nomination deadline autumn Nomination deadline spring Application deadline autumn Application deadline spring Period start the period concerned Period end the period concerned

You tick what you want to ask for: no need to claim six dates when two are enough.

Declared or guessed

A semester date attaches to an intake. The agenda tells you whether that intake was declared by the partner, or guessed from the date itself. The distinction matters when you build a campaign on it.

Your partner fills it in once

A reply is published, not addressed to you alone: the institution is talking about its own calendar, and its date reaches all of its partners. Periods are matched at read time, through their European coordinates — Vienna answers once, and every school with an autumn sees it.

One email per institution, to its main contact. The "Dates filled" column says where each one stands, and the orange warning names those with no main contact — they will receive nothing.

Use case.

In April, the coordinator asks her 62 partners for their nomination deadlines for both intakes. Three weeks later 48 have answered; she chases the other fourteen from the same screen, without writing an email.

docs.title: Finding your dates in Outlook
docs.text:
What it's for. Reading AroundLink's dates from the calendar you already use, without opening the tool.

Who it's for. the whole mobility team, and your students

How it works. AroundLink publishes your agenda in the standard format every calendar has been able to read for twenty years. You copy the subscription address, paste it into Outlook, and your dates appear — updating by themselves from then on.

This is not a Microsoft integration: it is an open format. Outlook, Google Calendar, Apple Calendar and the rest are served the same way, and your IT department has nothing to authorise or configure.

The subscription address is picked up under Settings ▸ Connectors ▸ Calendar, alongside the two other connections — see Emails & connectors.

Synchronisation only goes one way

Your calendar comes to read AroundLink's dates. It does not change them: a nomination deadline should not be movable from a student's Outlook. To change a date, go through the screen it comes from.

You subscribe to what you are looking at. The address carries the filters displayed when you copy it. So you can create several subscriptions — "my nominations" on one side, "the team's events" on the other — and see them as two separate calendars in Outlook, shown or hidden independently.

What the feed contains. Dates and their titles, nothing else. No student name and no personal data travel through this channel.

Use case.

The coordinator subscribes to their team's agenda filtered on outgoing students. Every Monday they see the week's deadlines in Outlook without opening AroundLink. When a date changes in the tool, their calendar follows.

The subscription address is personal

It gives access to your agenda, and only yours. Do not pass it on: anyone you gave it to would see your dates. Each person creates their own from their own account.

docs.title: Mobility grants (Erasmus+)
docs.text:
The Mobility grants module manages your institution's entire Erasmus+ financial side: annual allocation, grant allocation to students, payment tracking, supporting-document checklist and export to the official report. Erasmus+ rules (documents conditioning each payment, budget safeguards, per-country scales) are applied automatically, which safeguards your audits.

Paid-plan module

Mobility grants are part of AroundLink's paid offering. The module is only available to institutions that have subscribed to that plan.

docs.title: Finance dashboard
docs.text:
What it does. The module's landing page: a per-academic-year view combining the budget indicators, grant tracking and the case table, so the office has the Erasmus+ financial picture in front of them at a single glance.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator picks the academic year; the dashboard then shows the allocation, the amounts committed and paid, the remaining budget and the progress of the grant cases.

The agency allocation, what is committed and what remains, then each grant tracked by stage: agreement to sign, advance to pay, in mobility, missing documents, closed.

Use case.

At the start of the year, the coordinator opens the dashboard and sees at a glance how much of the allocation is already committed and how much remains available.

docs.title: Erasmus+ allocation (budget)
docs.text:
What it does. Records the institution's total Erasmus+ allocation for the academic year and shows consolidated figures in real time — allocation, amount committed to grants, amount actually paid, remaining balance — so the office never over-commits its funding.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator enters the allocation amount for the year; the module automatically computes and shows the committed amount, the paid amount and the remaining balance, consolidated at the institution level (all campuses combined).

Use case.

The coordinator records a €120,000 allocation; as grants are created, the dashboard shows €80,000 committed, €45,000 paid, €40,000 remaining.

docs.title: Grant management and lifecycle
docs.text:
What it does. The central grant record: one record per student per year, carrying the mobility type, dates, attributed amount, payments and the 7-item Erasmus+ checklist. Its status advances automatically as signatures and payments come in, so the office always knows where each case stands without manual bookkeeping.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator creates a grant for a student, enters the mobility type, dates and amount. The status is not set by hand: the case starts "awaiting agreement", then moves on its own to "active" once the grant agreement and the learning agreement are signed and the advance is paid, to "documents awaited" at the end of the mobility, and closes once all final documents are received.

Use case.

The coordinator creates a grant for a study mobility to Berlin; as the grant agreement and the learning agreement are signed and the advance paid, the grant moves on its own to "active", then closes itself once the certificate of attendance, the transcript and the final report are received.

docs.title: Budget safeguards
docs.text:
What it does. Prevents the office from allocating more grants than the Erasmus+ allocation allows, including when two coordinators act at the same time. Clearly distinguishes "allocation not set" (action needed) from "allocation exhausted".

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. When creating or editing a grant, the module checks that the requested amount does not exceed the remaining balance and blocks the operation if it would, with an explicit message. Only increases in commitment are blocked: correcting an amount downward or clearing it always remains possible.

Use case.

Two coordinators try at the same time to add €5,000 grants when only €6,000 remain: the first goes through, the second is rejected with "insufficient budget".

docs.title: Payment conditions
docs.text:
What it does. Applies the Erasmus+ rules that condition each payment tranche, so the office cannot record a payment before the required documents exist. Protects compliance in the event of an inspection.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. When recording a payment, the module blocks an increase of the advance as long as the grant agreement and the learning agreement are not signed, and an increase of the balance as long as the certificate of attendance and the final report are not received. It also ensures no payment is entered without an attributed amount and that the total paid does not exceed the attributed amount.

Use case.

The coordinator tries to record the advance before the learning agreement is signed: "Advance payment blocked — the grant agreement and the learning agreement must be signed first".

docs.title: Grant amount calculation
docs.text:
What it does. Computes the suggested grant amount from the official Erasmus+ scale (per-country monthly rate × duration, or daily rate for blended intensive programmes), so the office no longer computes amounts by hand and stays aligned with the national agency rates, revised every year.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. During entry, the module proposes an amount in real time from the institution, the mobility type and the dates. For a study or traineeship mobility, the calculation applies the host country's monthly rate to the duration; for a blended intensive programme, a daily rate to the duration in days.

Use case.

The coordinator enters a study mobility to Germany from 01/09 to 31/12; the form instantly shows the suggested amount, computed from the country-group rate and 4 months.

docs.title: Grant CSV import
docs.text:
What it does. Lets the office create many grants at once from a spreadsheet, rather than one by one, with a "check then confirm" flow that flags errors and warnings line by line and refuses any breach of the allocation.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator downloads a template file, fills it in, uploads it for preview — they get a per-line report (errors, warnings, suggested amount if the cell is empty) — then confirms to create the valid grants. An invalid line does not prevent the others from being imported.

Use case.

The coordinator imports 40 grants from a spreadsheet; 3 lines flag a breach of the allocation and are set aside, 37 are created.

docs.title: Export (Beneficiary Module) and audit log
docs.text:
What it does. Produces the rich CSV the office needs to report mobilities into the Erasmus+ Beneficiary Module (official organisation identities, ISCED subject area, participant data, unique mobility ID, distance band, derived indicators), as well as an export of the change log (who changed what, when) for internal audit.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator ; finance and compliance

How it works. The coordinator exports, for the chosen year, the grants CSV ready to be reported into the Beneficiary Module, and separately the audit log that traces each change with its author and date.

Use case.

At reporting time, the coordinator exports the year's grants to report them into the Beneficiary Module, and pulls the audit log for the internal auditor.

docs.title: Eligible-student picker
docs.text:
What it does. When creating a grant, only proposes students actually eligible for an Erasmus+ grant (active affectation to a programme country covered by the scale) and flags those who already have a grant, to avoid invalid or duplicate cases.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. In the creation window, the module shows the list of eligible students for the year and the institution, each with the suggested mobility type, the host institution, and an indication of whether they already have a grant.

Use case.

In the "new grant" window, the coordinator sees only the 22 eligible students; 3 already have a grant and are flagged as such.

docs.title: Mobility campaigns
docs.text: The Campaigns module structures application rounds: eligible students rank a set number of wishes among the catalogue's offers, and the IRO drives the whole thing — from opening to final placement — without rebuilding the list by hand.

docs.title: Mobility campaigns
docs.text:
What it's for. Lets an international relations office run a framed application round, where students rank a fixed number of exchange wishes within a given window. The campaign automatically determines which students and which partner offers belong to it, avoiding hand-picking each participant.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator creates a campaign by choosing the academic year, the number of allowed wishes, the target academic levels, the mobility periods, the eligible agreement types and an optional partner-tag filter. On save, the system builds the pool of participating students and the pool of eligible offers from those criteria. The campaign moves from Draft to Ready (opening it to students), then Opened and Finished; only a draft campaign remains editable.

The end date closes the campaign on its own. The morning after its last day, the campaign moves to Finished with nobody clicking: wishes still in draft become wishes, your students are notified and you receive the summary — exactly what the "Finish" button does.

If that closing feels premature, the "Reopen" button gives your students back the right to change their wishes. Remember to push the end date back: without that, the campaign closes again the next morning.

Your campaigns, whatever their status. The four counters at the top give you the state of play at a glance. Click the image to enlarge it.

Use case.

The IRO opens a "2026/2027 – Semester 1 – Master" campaign, 5 wishes allowed, restricted to Erasmus+ partners tagged "Engineering"; every Master student with a Semester 1 period is enrolled automatically.

docs.title: Setting up a campaign, setting by setting
docs.text:
What it's for. Understanding what each setting changes before you turn it on — several of them cannot be undone once your students have started answering.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Name, school year, opening and closing. The end cannot precede the start, and it is not decorative.

You choose the hour, not only the day. A campaign opens and closes to the minute: close at 18:00 and a wish submitted at 18:01 is refused. That is what lets you align a closing with a committee meeting rather than with an arbitrary midnight.

Screens show your institution's hour and name its timezone — yours and your students', not a server's.

Your gesture wins over the hour

If you reopen a campaign after its closing time, it stays open: the tool will not close it again a minute later. Push the closing back and it will close at the new time. In other words, automatic closing only fires at the moment the hour is crossed — never afterwards against your decision.

docs.title: The student pool
docs.text:
Who takes part. Combine as many criteria as you need:

  • Academic level and track — the track is the label you gave your cohorts ("Aero 4", "MSc 26-27");
  • Campus — or all of them;
  • General tags and student filters;
  • manual additions, student by student, for the odd case.

docs.title: The destination pool
docs.text:
Where they can go:

  • Agreement types — exchange, double degree, paying mobility, traineeship;
  • Mobility type — including staff mobility, teaching and training;
  • Periods;
  • Partners — all of them, or narrowed by your institution tags and filters.

Here too you can add or remove an agreement by hand.

docs.title: Wishes
docs.text: Minimum and maximum, both optional. The minimum blocks just as the maximum does: a student who has not reached the required number cannot submit their list.

docs.title: The student's file
docs.text:
You choose the required documents, then what happens when one is missing:

  • Show it and assign anyway (recommended) — the gap is flagged, the decision stays yours;
  • Block the assignment until everything is in hand.

docs.title: Can a student say they are not going?
docs.text:
• No — an empty wish list simply means "no answer yet";
  • Yes — they can declare they do not wish to go. They answer once, no reason is asked, and they immediately stop appearing in your reminders and in the matching. Their answer stays reversible while the campaign is open.

This setting cannot be caught up mid-course

A campaign that never asked the question does not start asking on its own. And once answers have come in, there is no going back — otherwise decisions your students already made would become unreadable.

docs.title: Who confirms the destination
docs.text:
• The student accepts or declines the proposal;
  • The coordinator assigns directly — the acceptance step disappears, your decision creates the placement.

docs.title: The mobility path
docs.text:
The Mobility workflow field plugs into the campaign the path its students will follow, from the partner's yes to their return. Only outgoing paths are offered.

It is optional: you can plug it in later from the campaign's Mobility tab. Without a path the campaign works — it simply gives its students no task after assignment.

docs.title: The note to students
docs.text: Free text, optional, shown to everyone taking part.

docs.title: The preview before saving
docs.text:
Before you confirm your changes, a summary tells you what the save will add, keep and remove — destinations as well as students. Removing a partner takes all of its agreements out of the campaign, along with the wishes already placed on them: the preview says so beforehand, not after.

A student only sees what is genuinely open to them

A destination appears in their list, and can be wished for, only if their row of the matrix — their year, their level, their track, their semester — declares places. A destination that is declared but full can still be wished for; one never opened to their promotion cannot.

You, the coordinator, keep all your freedom: adding a wish, pre-assigning, nominating — nothing changes on your side.

docs.title: What matching requires
docs.text:
What it's for. Knowing what must be ready for a matching round to run — and why it sometimes refuses to start.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The engine seats each student on the cell of their own track — "Aero 4" is not "Aero 5" — and it never guesses. Three conditions are therefore required of every participant:

Condition Why A profile With no file, there is nothing to place. A track It is what designates the cell. With no track, no cell matches them. An imported ranking The round is an order: it serves the first-ranked, and what is left goes to the next. With no rank, a student has no position in that order.

A participant missing any of the three is set aside and named in the report, with the reason. The round does not run in silence.

A track is required even if you do not use them

If your institution does not distinguish cohorts, give yourself one track per level you use — "Bachelor", "Master". A single mechanism then carries every case, and nothing is ever inferred on your behalf.

Rankings are imported beforehand, never during

The round does not produce a ranking. Import it first; otherwise unranked students would be served last, which would be a decision nobody took.

None of this constrains you by hand. You remain free to place whoever you want, wherever you want, ranked or not: that is your call, and the engine does not stand in the way. These three conditions apply to the automatic round only.

A round can be re-run as often as needed — it is not a one-shot.

docs.title: Wishes, proposals and placements
docs.text:
What it's for. Turns each student's ranked wish list into a confirmed placement, respecting real place availability and student rank. Automates the "who goes where" allocation offices otherwise run on spreadsheets, while letting the coordinator adjust and the student accept or refuse.

Who it's for. coordinator / student

How it works. Students submit an ordered wish list. The coordinator launches automatic allocation, which processes students by rank (GPA) and offers each the first wish that still has a place for their period; those who can't be placed are flagged. The coordinator can then pre-assign (override), refuse or cancel a proposal — each action recalculates the rest — then send proposals to students, who accept (creating a nomination to the partner) or refuse (which cancels their other wishes and frees the place). When a proposal is sent or a student is placed, they can be notified — by email and/or in the app; these notifications are configurable and can be turned off by the institution.

A campaign's tracking: at the top, what it holds, what is placed and how wishes were met; below, your students in ranking order, with their wishes as they ranked them.

Use case.

Two students rank Berlin as wish #1: the higher-ranked one (GPA) gets the proposal, the other automatically rolls to their wish #2. The coordinator then pre-assigns a special case, and the system redistributes the freed place.

docs.title: What the matching round did
docs.text:
What it's for. Knowing exactly what a matching round placed, what it could not place, and who it left aside.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. At the end of the round, a report tells you how many students were served and which ones were left out. Skipped students are named, with the reason — a bare total would send you through the whole cohort to find them.

Four reasons can leave a student aside:

  • they have no profile;
  • their level has no track attached;
  • they have no ranking;
  • their file is incomplete.

A round that places nobody now says so plainly, instead of reporting itself as completed.

Use case.

The coordinator runs the round and reads the report: forty-two students placed, three left out for want of a ranking. It names them; they import the ranks and run the round again.

docs.title: Tracking, results and exports
docs.text:
What it's for. Gives the coordinator an operational dashboard of the running campaign (who submitted, who's placed, dossier completeness), results and accepted views, plus CSV exports for downstream processing. A campaign becomes a traceable, usable process.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The tracking page aggregates participants, their wishes by rank, proposals and placements, with charts and a completed-dossier counter. Wishes are also grouped by geographic zone — Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia-Oceania, Africa, Middle East — so you can read at a glance where demand is going. Dedicated pages present results and accepted students, and two exports produce the all-wishes list and the final-assignments list.

Counter accuracy. Destination and institution counts only include what is genuinely open to students: hidden or archived partners are excluded, as are destinations with no place available. The figures shown match what the student will see.

Use case.

Mid-round, the coordinator sees 60% of students have submitted their wishes and 12 are placed; after closing, they export the final assignments for the mobility team.

docs.title: The Mobility tab: after the assignment
docs.text:
What it's for. Tracking stopped at the assignment. The Mobility tab takes over: it shows what placed students are doing, from the partner's answer to their return.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The tab opens like the three others and carries mobility tracking: table or kanban, the three phases, the search that suggests filters, the export of what is on screen.

If no path is plugged in, the tab says what is missing and where to set it — and lets you plug it in without leaving the screen. Changing the path of a campaign in service asks for confirmation: students under way switch to the new one.

Removing a wish, even one the student added

The coordinator can remove any wish, including those the student added themselves. Removing a student-added wish asks for an explicit confirmation.

docs.title: Nominating to your partners
docs.text:
What it's for. Officially telling the host institution you are sending them a student, then recording their answer.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. Each row is a student assigned to a destination. You nominate them, and the partner is informed. When they reply, you record their decision, stating how it reached you: the platform, the EWP network, an email or a phone call. A refusal comes with its reason.

The tab appears as soon as a place is held in the campaign. You can nominate a whole selection in one go: the batch is processed in slices, its progress stays visible, and an interrupted batch resumes where it stopped instead of starting over.

What the partner receives. A message in your colours — your logo, your name, the signature of the person following the file — listing the nominated students with their level, and nothing else. A nomination of eight students goes out as one message, not eight. The recipient receives an access to their own space, created without a separate invitation: they find there the files you send them and your fiche, never the rest of your space.

With no reachable contact, the nomination does not go out

The message goes to the partner's main contact; failing that, to the agreement's signatory, then to the agreement's contact. If none of the three is filled in, the student stays pending and the screen points you to the partner's Contacts tab.

While the partner has not replied, two actions save you leaving the tool:

  • Remind — a reminder goes to the partner without going through your mailbox. One reminder per twenty-four hours: the button greys out afterwards.
  • Withdraw — you cancel the nomination and say why. The partner is told no decision is expected any more, and the student becomes available for another destination.

The automatic reminder

A nomination left unanswered beyond the delay you set — six days by default, adjustable from 1 to 60 — is reminded once, automatically. It has its own counter: it does not consume your manual reminder, so you can still remind by hand the same day. An accepted, refused or withdrawn nomination is never reminded.

Each nomination's state and, for confirmed ones, how the answer came in.

Use case.

The coordinator nominates twelve students; eight confirmations come back through the platform or EWP, two by phone which they record by hand, and one destination refuses for lack of a place in the requested specialisation.

Document reminders

Automatic reminders to students with an incomplete dossier are covered by document reminders.

docs.title: Exporting nominations for the EWP Dashboard
docs.text:
What it's for. Avoiding double entry. Fifty students nominated in AroundLink, and fifty entries typed by hand into the Dashboard: the export produces the file in the expected format.

How it works. The Export button on the tracking page gathers every export and then asks which one. The nominations export opens a preview before download, which says:

  • how many rows will go;
  • who stays behind, and why — a student left out is named, never lost in silence;
  • how many already went in a previous file — they do not go twice;
  • and if the export is empty, the reason: students hold a place but are not nominated yet.

What goes, and what does not

The export only takes nominations awaiting an answer: a nomination already confirmed has no business in the Dashboard. Traineeships stay out, and subject areas are checked before the file is written.

docs.title: A campaign's statistics
docs.text:
What it's for. Knowing where a campaign stands, why some students are not placed, and producing a report you can take to a committee.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. Statistics have their own address: a tab in their own right, at the same level as wish management and nominations. You can send the link to a colleague, and they will land on the same figures.

Everything shown comes from the same source as the placement screen. Tables and charts cannot contradict each other.

The headline figures. The placement rate, the average wish obtained, and the breakdown of those still waiting: awaiting a decision, all wishes refused, mobility declined, cancelled. Each line is a different thing to do — reminding a student who is waiting is not the same gesture as handling one whose every wish was refused.

The breakdowns. By agreement type, by country, by zone, by period.

Demand and tension per destination: where the crowd is, and where room is left.

Two rules that stop the figures from flattering

The average wish obtained is computed on placed students only. Saying "80% got their first choice" while counting everyone would flatter a campaign that placed nobody.

A breakdown of fewer than five students is not shown. On a small cohort, a percentage is one person: it reads as a trend when it is an anecdote.

The four headline figures, the wish obtained by rank, "why they are not placed", then the breakdowns by country, zone, agreement type and period — and tension destination by destination.

The report prints. The header recalls the campaign's settings — school year, opening dates, mobility type, number of wishes allowed, who confirms the destination, whether an incomplete file blocks — and repeats at the top of every page, with your logo and the date. Charts survive printing, and a block that does not fit moves to the next page instead of being cut.

Both pages of the report as it comes out: the campaign's settings at the top, the four figures, the rank of wish obtained and the reasons for not being placed; then tension destination by destination.

Download a sample report — PDF, 2 pages, demonstration data.

The data export. Alongside the report, a three-sheet workbook:

Sheet What it holds Students One row per student: class rank, identity, level, track, year, language scores, then each wish with its code, university, city, country, place type and period By university The same campaign seen by destination Final assignments The placements retained

Download a sample workbook — Excel, 3 sheets, identities replaced with sample values.

The report is for showing, the workbook for working on: one goes to the committee, the other into a spreadsheet.

Use case.

Before the committee meets, the coordinator opens the statistics, prints the report to PDF and attaches it to the invitation. Members arrive having seen the same figures she has, and the discussion is about the twelve unplaced students rather than about reading tables.

docs.title: Communications & notifications
docs.text: This module brings together everything about the International Relations Office's communication: broadcasting a message to a targeted audience, notifying in real time, chatting directly with a student or partner, and automatically chasing missing documents. The goal: replace scattered manual emailing with integrated, tracked tools.

docs.title: Broadcast messaging
docs.text:
What it's for. You write a message once and broadcast it across several channels — in-app notification, email, dashboard pin, direct message — to targeted audiences. No more manual mail-merge: you target, you send, and you keep a record.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. The composer lets you choose the audiences (outgoing students, incoming students, partners) and optional filters (country, campus, student access status), with a live recipient counter before sending. You can also start from an explicit selection: tick the students you want in your list, or the contacts you want in your directory, and send to those alone — useful when the group you have in mind matches no filter. You select the channels you want, you can save a draft, and a sent message is locked. On send, a receipt shows the number of recipients, emails sent and pinned messages. A pinned message can later be removed from the dashboard.

Composing a broadcast: subject, message, target audience, optional filters and sending channels.

Use case.

A coordinator sends "Nomination deadline extended to March 15" to all outgoing students in Spain, pinned to their dashboard and sent by email.

docs.title: The identity of your emails
docs.text:
What it's for. Many of the messages leaving AroundLink reach people who are not your users: a partner, a contact, a student who has not signed in yet. They recognise the school they work with, not a tool they have never heard of.

How it works. Every message therefore carries your logo and your name at the top, the signature of the person sending it at the bottom of the card, and a discreet powered by AroundLink on the right. An email is written by one person to one person, not by a system.

Four exceptions

Messages nobody sends — password reset, generic message — keep our mark alone. A "powered by" line only makes sense behind someone else's name.

docs.title: In-app notifications
docs.text:
What it's for. Every user has a notification feed with a live unread counter in the top bar. Coordinators, partners and students stay informed of new messages and events without relying on email.

Who it's for. coordinator / partner / student

How it works. The bell shows the number of unread notifications; opening one marks it read, and a button lets you mark all read at once. A notification can link back to its source message.

Use case.

A student sees a "3" on the bell, opens it and finds their Learning Agreement has just been approved.

docs.title: Direct messaging
docs.text:
What it's for. Private threaded messaging between the three actor types — IR team, students, AroundLink team. Questions get settled inside the platform rather than through scattered emails.

Who it's for. coordinator / student / partner

How it works. Each profile has its own inbox: a conversation list, a one-to-one thread with read-on-open, reply, and a "new message" picker to start an exchange. An unread counter shows in the top bar.

Use case.

An incoming student writes to the host office with a housing question; the coordinator replies in the thread.

docs.title: Document reminder campaigns
docs.text:
What it's for. Automated, tracked reminder-email campaigns nudge students to submit their missing documents, with open, click and bounce statistics per campaign. Chasing documents becomes a measurable, one-click operation.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. A campaign targets students by document type, study level and related campaigns. The campaign list and a statistics window show the number of emails sent, the open rate, the click rate and the delivery rate. Emails then go out automatically as a background task.

Use case.

A coordinator launches a reminder for all Master students missing their Learning Agreement, then checks a 62% open rate in the statistics window.

From campaigns

Reminders can also be triggered from the document tracking of a campaign: it's the same reminder mechanism documented here.

docs.title: Feedback request reminders
docs.text:
What it's for. Prompt students who have not yet left a review about their host institution, on the same principle as document reminders.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. You target your audience by study level and campaign, or you name the students directly — naming students then takes precedence over the filters. A preview tells you how many people will be reached before sending, and that number matches exactly who receives the message.

Students who have already answered drop out of the reminder on their own: no need to keep a list by hand.

Use case.

At the end of the semester, the coordinator reminds returning Master's students who have not left a review yet; the preview announces 12 recipients, and 12 messages go out.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The dashboard is your team's home page: what needs acting on today, and where your mobility stands as a whole.

docs.title: Your student pipeline
docs.text:
What it's for. Seeing where your students sit along their path, and spotting where it gets stuck.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. A nineteen-bar histogram, spread over the five stages of a mobility — access, campaign, preparation, mobility, after — each with its own colour.

You switch between your outgoing and incoming students, then pick the view: each button on the second row is a campaign, and the histogram shows only its students.

The bars do not add up — and that is deliberate

The first nine, those of access and campaign, are mutually exclusive: a student is either "no access" or "connected", never both.

From preparation onwards they are checklist items: one student in mobility can raise five bars at once — agreement validated, documents complete, arrival certificate. That is why no total is shown: it would mean nothing.

Use case.

The coordinator switches to her spring campaign and sees "awaiting proposal" climb to forty-eight while "proposal" stays at zero. The matching round has not been run yet.

A coordinator's dashboard: the pipeline and its five colours, the four counters for today, places distributed by period and track, where the agreements come from, and at the bottom the tiles of what awaits validation.

docs.title: Today's figures
docs.text:
How it works. Four counters at the top of the page: your outgoing students, with how many are abroad today; your incoming ones, with those on campus; your active partners; your contacts.

These are figures for right now, not year totals.

docs.title: Places distributed
docs.text:
How it works. A cross-table: your periods as rows — autumn, spring, full year, summer — and your tracks as columns, with the total for the chosen school year at the top. You change year from a menu.

It is the overview of what you have opened, before going into one agreement's matrix.

docs.title: Where your agreements come from
docs.text:
How it works. A ring splits your agreements by family — Erasmus+, bilateral, double degree, paying mobility — with each one's share.

Use case.

The manager sees that 56% of their agreements are Erasmus+ and 7% paying mobility, and decides to balance the network next year.

docs.title: What is waiting on you
docs.text:
What it's for. Starting your day with what is blocking somebody else.

How it works. A row of tiles mirrors the validation queue's own buckets: learning agreements, nominations, transcripts, language scores, feedback, grant documents, other documents.

Each tile opens the queue already filtered on its bucket. Clicking a precise number only to land on an unfiltered three-hundred-row list would be a click you then have to undo.

Three families of documents, not one

Documents are split the way the queue splits them: a grant certificate blocking a payment is not a CV. Grouping them would bury the urgent one in the pile.

Use case.

Monday morning, the "learning agreements" tile reads twelve. One click, and the queue opens on those twelve, ready to validate.

docs.title: The search bar
docs.text:
What it's for. Finding a person or an institution from any screen, without going through the right list first.

Who it's for. the whole mobility team

How it works. The search ignores accents, both ways: "Bergstrom" finds "Bergström", and the other way round too. A name starting with É, À, Ü, Ö or Ç is found like any other.

Each result carries the fact that places it, rather than an email address that tells nothing apart between eleven namesakes:

  • a student — their school when you have several, otherwise their address, then their number;
  • an institution — its country spelled out and the agreement family that links you;
  • a contact — the institution they belong to.

Results are ranked by relevance, and a counter says how many there are in total.

Three letters are enough. Results are grouped by family with their counter — students, contacts — and each carries the fact that places it.

A useful side effect

Because both spellings now meet, a single word typed without accents surfaces the duplicates nobody could see — "Bahçeşehir Üniversitesi" and "Bahcesehir University" come out together.

docs.title: Steering indicators
docs.text:
What it's for. The underlying trends, for decisions from one year to the next rather than for this week.

Who it's for. international office management

How it works. Below the operational blocks, a set of steering indicators: mobility growth, the most requested destinations, place occupancy, inclusion and fewer-opportunities groups.

They are read-only and cover your institution alone.

docs.title: Documents & templates
docs.text: What your institution asks for and what it produces: the document types required from your students, and the templates of the official documents the platform generates in their name. It is a setting — done once, then it applies to every file.

docs.title: Document templates
docs.text:
What it does. Lets each institution design its own reusable document templates (nomination letter, learning agreement, acceptance letter, enrolment certificate, transcript of records, visa certificate, housing certificate) with {{…}} fields that fill automatically with a student's real data.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator lists, creates and edits their templates, composes the document body using the available variables, previews the layout as a PDF (tokens still visible) to check spacing and pagination, then generates a filled PDF for a given student. They can activate/deactivate a template or delete it. Institutional templates made available are visible read-only.

Your generated document templates — acceptance letter, enrolment certificate, learning agreement, transcript — where the student's details replace the variables.

Use case.

The coordinator creates an "Acceptance Letter" template with the institution's logo, checks the preview, then generates it filled for an incoming student in one click.

docs.title: Enable / disable document types
docs.text:
What it does. Lets each institution enable or disable certain document types, so an unwanted type stops appearing on the students' upload page and in dropdown lists. By default, all types are active.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. In Settings → Documents, each document type has an ON/OFF switch saved per institution.

The documents your institution asks for, by family. Turning a type off removes it from the student's profile without deleting anything already uploaded.

Use case.

An institution that never issues housing certificates disables that type: it disappears from every student's checklist.

docs.title: Emails & connectors
docs.text:
Exchanges with your partners live in your mail client, and the student's file lives in AroundLink. Filed emails bring the two together: a message exchanged with a contact ends up on their fiche, with nobody retyping anything.

Where it happens

Settings ▸ Connectors brings the three connections together: Email, Calendar and API. Filed messages are then read on the fiches — partner, contact, student.

docs.title: Filing your emails without leaving Outlook
docs.text:
What it is for. Finding, six months later, what was said to a partner — without digging through the mailbox of a colleague who is on holiday.

Who it is for. the whole mobility team

How it works. An Outlook add-in files the emails you exchange with your contacts on the right fiche, from your mail client. A message is filed only when it is authenticated and involves a contact already in AroundLink; everything else is read and forgotten.

Installation takes six steps, given directly on the page — Microsoft only allows an add-in to be added from a buried page of its own site, and the second half of the guide (where to click in Outlook once the add-in is in place) appears in no Microsoft documentation. Every delicate step carries its screenshot.

  1. download the add-in file — a single file, to keep until step 3;
  2. open your Outlook add-ins, left column, My add-ins;
  3. under Custom add-ins, Add a custom add-in, then Add from file;
  4. open an email, then the Apps button in the message toolbar;
  5. pick AroundLink for Outlook from the list;
  6. pin the pane, so it stays open from one message to the next.

Without the add-in: the address in Cc

If the add-in is not an option, put your institution's address in Cc when you write to a contact: the message lands on their fiche. One button copies it from the Connectors page. It is a fallback, not the solution: you have to remember it on every message, which is the whole reason the add-in exists.

docs.title: Reading exchanges on a fiche
docs.text:
What it is for. Seeing the history of a relationship where you actually work.

How it works. Filed messages appear identically on three screens: a partner's fiche, under Relationship ▸ All emails (the aggregate of its contacts' emails), a contact's fiche, and a student's fiche, under Emails.

  • one card per message, only one open at a time;
  • the direction of the exchange is marked — received or sent;
  • names are links when the person is on file with you; an unknown address stays plain text, which is the truth;
  • attachments download from the card;
  • Reply and Forward open your mail client with the message quoted.

On a student's fiche, emails are matched to their addresses — the school one and the personal one. The list there is read-only: a message is managed from the fiche of the contact that carries it.

In contact grids, a Last contact column gives the date of the latest exchange.

Nothing is deleted there

The email screens carry no destructive gesture. A message filed by mistake is handled on the administration side, not from a fiche — a relationship history that one click could empty would not be a history.

docs.title: The calendar and the API
docs.text:
How it works. The two other connections live in the same place.

  • Calendar — read your AroundLink agenda from Outlook, Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The link carries your whole agenda and reads one way only: your calendar comes to read, it changes nothing.
  • API — let your own systems read and write AroundLink data. This connection is meant for your institution's IT team. The key is personal, not your institution's: everyone has their own, and regenerating it leaves a colleague's working.

Use case.

The head of office writes to her counterpart in Bologna to settle the semester dates. The AroundLink pane is pinned in her Outlook: the message is filed on the contact's fiche. Three months later, her colleague opens the partner's fiche, reads the exchange, and replies from the card without searching her own mailbox.

docs.title: Incoming students
docs.text: The students you host, including those your partners nominate to you. The ones you send have their own list, and each of them has their file.

docs.title: Incoming students
docs.text:
What it's for. Following the students your partners send you, from nomination through to the end of their stay.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator
