How it works. Two tabs separate what is offered to you from what you have accepted: Nominations for proposals awaiting your decision, My students for those you are actually hosting. An incoming student appears from the moment they are nominated, before they even have an account.

Once you accept the nomination, you open their access: they receive their credentials and can complete their file. The list sorts, filters and tags exactly like the outgoing one.

Your incoming students, with their level, their year and the state of their connection to the platform.

Use case.

A partner university nominates twelve students; the coordinator accepts eleven, refuses one, then opens access for the eleven retained.

docs.title: Outgoing students
docs.text: The students you send on mobility. The ones you host have their own list, and each of them has their file.

docs.title: Outgoing students
docs.text:
What it's for. Finding all of your institution's students going on mobility, following where each one stands, and acting on several of them at once.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. Each row is a student. The list sorts and filters on every column — level, campus, year, campaigns, tags, access status. The Access column shows where their account stands: never sent, sending, or connected.

Select several students and you can open their access, apply or remove tags, send an email, an internal message or a reminder — all in one operation. The list can be imported from and exported to a spreadsheet.

Your outgoing students. The top bar appears as soon as you make a selection and gathers the actions that apply to the whole batch. Click the image to enlarge it.

Use case.

The coordinator filters on the Master cohort, selects the 40 students concerned and opens their platform access in one go.

Nominating a student

Nominating to a partner does not start from this list: it happens from the campaign, once the student has been assigned to a destination.

docs.title: A student's record
docs.text: Outgoing or incoming, every student has a fiche gathering their whole file: identity, documents, learning agreement, transcript, mobility tracking. You reach it from the list of outgoing or incoming students.

docs.title: A student's file
docs.text:
What it's for. Bringing together everything about one student: their identity, their documents, their learning agreement, their transcript, their grant and their reviews.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. Click a row to open the file. Tabs separate the main parts of the record. The Overview tab gathers their identity, contact details, academic information, their GPA and their cohort ranking where those have been imported.

A student's overview: identification, identity, contacts and academic information.

Use case.

Before confirming a nomination, the coordinator opens the file to check the student's language level and GPA.

docs.title: The Mobility tab
docs.text:
What it's for. Answering, when you open a file, the question you actually ask: where does this student stand, and do I have anything to do?

How it works. The Mobility tab carries one block per mobility — a student who left twice has two files, each with its dates and its progress. You read the phase, the tasks sorted by phase, and the dated timeline of the stay. It is the same screen as mobility tracking, seen at the scale of one student.

docs.title: Email exchanges
docs.text:
What it's for. Reading, on the fiche, what has been written to the student, without leaving their file.

How it works. An Emails tab matches filed messages to the student's addresses — the school one and the personal one. The list is read-only: a message is managed from the fiche of the contact that carries it. See Emails & connectors.

In the grids, a Last contact column gives the date of the latest exchange, and a student's name always leads to their fiche.

docs.title: Removing a language test
docs.text: How it works. A cross lets the coordinator remove a language test from a student's fiche — a document uploaded by mistake, an expired certificate. It is one of the actions the coordinator can take on the student's behalf when they cannot manage.

docs.title: Student profile completion
docs.text:
What it's for. Seeing at a glance which students have not finished filling in their profile, and reminding them without keeping a list.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. Completion is measured on the nine pieces of information only the student can give about themselves: date, place and country of birth, nationality, gender, personal email, phone number, emergency number and profile photo.

What you fill in yourself — first name, last name, student number, institutional email, level — does not count: a student should not be measured on someone else's work.

You find this measure in the Profile column of your student list, which sorts and filters like the others. The student sees a gauge on their profile and a window offering to complete what is missing, field by field.

Once the list is filtered on incomplete profiles, the reminder goes out from the selection bar, like any other reminder.

Use case.

Three weeks before departures, the coordinator sorts their list on the Profile column, selects the twenty-two students below 100%, and sends a reminder. Each one receives the list of their own missing fields.

Gender left unanswered

"Not answered" is the record's default value, not an answer: the gauge does not count it. A student who would rather not answer picks "Prefer not to say", which does count as an answer — otherwise they would stay below 100% forever.

docs.title: A student's documents
docs.text:
What it's for. Seeing at a glance what the student has provided, what is still missing, and acting on each item.

Who it's for. IRO manager / coordinator

How it works. The Documents tab lists every item your institution asks for, grouped by family — identity and administrative, academic, financial. Each card shows whether the item is provided, validated or still expected, and whether it is required or optional.

Students upload their own documents; you view them, download them, then approve or refuse them. You can also upload an item on their behalf — a score received directly from the test centre, for instance — in which case it is recorded as validated, and the file keeps track of who uploaded it.

A student's documents, by family, with their status and the language scores recorded.

Use case.

The coordinator receives a student's language certificate by post, uploads it to her file themselves, and the item immediately shows as validated.

Approving in batches

To handle everything your students have submitted in one place, go through validations rather than file by file.

docs.title: Learning Agreement (OLA)
docs.text:
What it does. The Learning Agreement describes the programme of courses a student will follow abroad. This view lets the office track every agreement, see at a glance which ones are pending, validated or need corrections, and enforce the signature of both institutions before an agreement becomes final.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator opens the OLA list, filters by status and reviews each agreement in a window that shows its history. They can request modifications — the agreement then returns to draft with a comment for the student — or approve it. For a standard agreement, each institution signs on its own side, in any order, and the agreement is validated only once both signatures are in place; for an EWP agreement, approval hands the agreement to the host institution following the network's sequential flow.

Use case.

The coordinator reviews Marie's pre-departure OLA (3 courses, 18 ECTS), asks her to swap one course, then signs on behalf of the sending institution; as soon as the partner signs in turn, the OLA becomes "Validated".

docs.title: The coordinator corrects, instead of only judging
docs.text:
What it does. A contract refused over a comma meant a full round trip: comment, wait, new submission, new review. When the correction is obvious, it may as well be made.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A pencil on the OLA tab opens the correction. The coordinator can:

  • correct the contract's period and language;
  • correct the course list, drawing from the partner's catalogue;
  • add a free course, when the course is not in the catalogue.

The OLA tab now opens the contract directly, instead of asking for one more click.

A student who had signed is told

If the contract already carried their signature, they are told they must resubmit: a signature only covers the text signed. The contract does not become validated behind their back.

On an EWP agreement, the amendment stays closed

For a contract travelling on the European network, correction by the coordinator is not open: the network imposes its own amendment circuit, and two paths for the same change would produce two versions of the contract.

docs.title: The documents of an incoming student hosted on a campus
docs.text: How it works. When you host a student on one of your campuses, their documents — learning agreement and transcript — carry "School — Campus" rather than the institution's name alone. The student and their home school therefore know where the stay actually took place.

docs.title: PDF generation: OLA & transcript of records
docs.text:
What it does. Produces the official PDF of the learning agreement or the transcript of records from the institution's document template (letterhead, layout), with the student's course table inserted automatically. The office gets a document ready to file, in the institution's colours.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. From the OLA list, the coordinator downloads the PDF of the learning agreement or the transcript of records. The agreement can only be downloaded once fully validated; the transcript once the transcript itself is validated. The system fills the template with the courses (and the grades, for the transcript).

Use case.

After both signatures, the coordinator downloads the Learning Agreement as a PDF, on the institution's letterhead, for the student's file.

docs.title: Transcript of Records (ToR)
docs.text:
What it does. Manages the incoming student's transcript that the host institution must return to the home institution. The coordinator reviews the entered grades and the uploaded official transcript, then validates or requests corrections.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator (validation) ; student (entry)

How it works. The student enters each grade according to the chosen grading system and uploads the official transcript. The coordinator opens the transcript in a window showing the history and the uploaded document, then validates — the transcript becomes downloadable — or sends the file back to the student for correction.

Use case.

An incoming student uploads their official transcript and enters their grades; the coordinator checks, validates, and the transcript of records is ready to be sent to the home university.

docs.title: Your public page
docs.text:
Your public page is a web page in your name, reachable without an account, that you compose from AroundLink and hand to whoever you like: a partner discovering you, a student hesitating, a colleague preparing a committee.

It reuses what you already maintain in the tool — your photos, your mobility periods, your language requirements, your course catalogue, your FAQ. Nothing to retype.

Where it happens

My institution ▸ Public page. The page's address is app.aroundlink.com/aroundlink/<your-school>.

docs.title: Composing, not filling in a form
docs.text:
What it is for. Deciding what the world sees of you, while seeing it.

Who it is for. IO officer / coordinator

How it works. The composer shows the page itself, exactly as the public will see it. The preview is the page: there is no "edit mode" that would render differently from reality.

Everything is published by default. There is nothing to tick to get started: the moment you switch your page on, all your sections are there. The left panel is there to remove what you do not want to show, section by section or whole category — not to build the page item by item.

The direction of travel is the point: the tool publishes what you already maintain, and you keep the hand to hide part of it.

On the left, your sections: a switch and a counter each, on by default. In the middle, the page as the public will see it; at the top left, the campus selector.

The order of sections cannot be changed

That is deliberate: every institution's page reads in the same order, which makes it comparable from one partner to the next. You decide what you hide, not the order.

docs.title: What you can put on it
docs.text:
How it works. Your logo is served automatically, at the top and in the footer: it is not a block to tick. The rest is your choice.

Group Available blocks Identity & media Photos · Key facts (website, Erasmus code, accreditations) · Campus cards Academic data Mobility periods · Language requirements · Course catalogue · Catalogue filter by promotion Your sections every section of your student content, in the order of your categories — general information, academic aspects, student life, scholarships, logistics FAQ your frequently asked questions, which close the page Side panel Nomination and application deadlines · Team contacts (role and email only) · Postal address · Student reviews (no names) · Useful links

What never goes out

Team contacts only expose the role and the email address — never a personal number. Student reviews are published without their author's name. And no content belonging to another institution appears on your page.

The same page, seen without an account: your colours and logo in the banner, the table of contents on the left, and the panel carrying your next deadlines, your address, your students' reviews and your links.

A full example, to scroll through

Open a sample public page — the whole page of a demonstration institution, from the introduction to the FAQ. It is a frozen copy: the links in it lead nowhere.

docs.title: Your colours
docs.text:
How it works. You set two colours — an accent colour and a dark one — and the page follows: the banner, the buttons, the footer. With your logo opening and closing the page, it looks like your institution, not like AroundLink.

A discreet Powered by AroundLink signature sits at the bottom.

docs.title: One page per campus
docs.text:
What it is for. An institution with several sites has more than one reality: courses, periods and contacts may differ from one city to the next.

How it works. Each declared campus can have its own page, composed separately, and a selector moves from one to another in the composer. Content is broken down by campus: a course declares which campuses it is taught on, and a campus page only shows its own.

On the public side, a menu links the pages together. A campus address is shared as you are looking at it.

docs.title: Publishing, sharing, switching off
docs.text:
How it works. One switch publishes the page. The address copies with a button.

The address never regenerates

That is deliberate: you must be able to leave this link everywhere — in your emails, on your website, in a printed PDF — without it breaking one day. If you no longer want to be visible, switch the page off: that is the fallback, and the link works again when you switch it back on.

Use case.

The office composes its page in twenty minutes: photos, periods, language requirements, course catalogue, FAQ, and in the side panel the two nomination deadlines. It sets the school's colours, publishes, and pastes the address into its email signature. A partner asking "your dates and prerequisites?" now gets a link instead of a PDF.

docs.title: My institution (Resource Hub)
docs.text: "My institution" is the space where the International Relations Office keeps up to date all the practical information its outgoing and incoming students will see: identity, factsheet, courses, useful links, a document library and FAQs. Here you see your institution exactly as your partners see it, and you moderate the published student reviews.

docs.title: "My institution" content editor
docs.text:
What it's for. This is the single place to keep the student-facing knowledge base current. You manage the institution's identity and all its practical content, with visibility adjustable per audience (incoming, outgoing, free mobility). One place to keep the information students see accurate and up to date.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. The page is organized into four tabs. Information: identity fields (code, name, country…), the logo, accreditations, your language requirements and your agenda. Student Info: your content for students — factsheet, courses and programmes, links, library, reviews and FAQ — where each item carries its visibility audiences. Contacts: your team and your counterparts. Public page: composing your public page.

A vertical index lists the sections with, next to each, what is left to fill in — 17/17 when everything is there. Content is written as blocks attached to categories and sub-categories.

Your student content: the index of sections and their counters on the left, the written blocks on the right. The pencil edits, the bin removes.

Your EWP factsheet stays apart, under its own screen: that is the one the European network publishes.

Your factsheet as your partners read it: websites, nomination and application deadlines per term, incoming coordinators and the procedure to follow. The banner at the top says whether the data came from an EWP sync or from your own entry, and the padlock locks a section so a sync cannot overwrite it.

Use case.

A coordinator adds a "Cost of living in Lisbon" link visible only to incoming students, then uploads a welcome PDF to the library.

Student side

The documents and resources you make visible appear in the "Resources" area of the student portal — see the student-portal documentation.

docs.title: Factsheet, courses, links, library and FAQ
docs.text:
What it's for. These sub-tabs make up the practical content a student consults before and during mobility: institution overview, course offer, external links, downloadable documents and frequently asked questions.

How it works. Each sub-tab offers full management (add, edit, delete) of its items, with per-audience visibility settings. The library accepts downloadable files; the FAQ is authored as question-and-answer pairs.

docs.title: IIA factsheet (EWP)
docs.text:
What it's for. The "IIA factsheet" tab shows your own institution's EWP factsheet — the one the network and your partners consult: nomination calendar, coordinators, contact information. You keep it synchronized from this screen.

How it works. The tab displays your EWP factsheet and its associated information (sync, calendar, coordinators). It's the "our side" counterpart of the factsheet you consult at a partner.

docs.title: Announcing your language requirements to your whole network
docs.text:
What it's for. Your language prerequisites change from one year to the next. Rather than waiting for each partner to ask, you announce them in one gesture.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

Two numbered requirements, each with its language. The word between them is clickable, to switch from "and" to "or". Under each, the accepted tests — "any one of these is enough".

How it works. Sending happens in two steps, like publishing your dates: you look first at what would go out and to how many partners, then you send. A message to fifty universities cannot be taken back; the number of recipients is in front of you before the click, not in the report afterwards.

The screen also reminds you when you last announced.

The counterpart: asking a partner for theirs

From a partner's fiche, you can ask for their language requirements through a link that needs no account. They fill in their prerequisites, language by language, and these appear on their fiche. The form carries your logo, so they know who is asking. A notification tells you as soon as they have answered.

Before sending: what your partners will read, how many will receive the email, and — named one by one — those left out for want of a main contact.

Use case.

In June, the office raises its English requirement from B2 to C1. It opens the preview, sees the announcement would go to 47 partners, and sends it. No email to write.

docs.title: What you still have to fill in
docs.text:
What it's for. An empty fiche does not announce itself. The index counters say what each section contains — never what is missing, nor what it costs. An institution can go months without its website filled in: one field, one click, and nothing ever told them.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A pill appears at the bottom right of your screens, with the number of things left:

At the bottom right, discreet and always there as long as something remains.

It opens a list where each line says what to do and, above all, what it changes:

What is missing What it costs Your contact details students and partners have no way to reach you Your semester dates partners email you to ask Your language levels students apply without knowing if they qualify Photos of your campus your page opens on an empty banner Your course catalogue students can't build a learning agreement

What is left and what is done. Each line names the consequence, not a percentage.

No gauge, no percentage

"You are at 36%" does not say what to do. A line that states the consequence does — that is what makes you act, never the figure.

It disappears when nothing is left

There is no "all done" state: when the list is empty, the pill leaves the screen. A reminder you cannot silence becomes furniture, and you stop seeing it — including the day it has something to say.

docs.title: Student-review moderation
docs.text:
What it's for. You collect reviews from students returning from mobility (rating, topic, free text, photos) and moderate them before they appear to future students. It's a trusted, first-hand review layer to help with destination choice.

Who it's for. coordinator / IR manager

How it works. A review carries a rating, a topic, the author's name, the country type, content and optional photos. From the "feedback" sub-tab, you accept or refuse each contribution; accepted, public reviews then surface to students.

The reviews left about your institution, split between pending, accepted and refused. Each carries its topic, rating and author, and you choose to accept it internally, accept and publish it, or refuse it.

Use case.

A student back from Antalya leaves a 4-star review with photos; the coordinator approves it, and it shows on the Antalya page for next year's applicants.

docs.title: Opening a campus as a destination
docs.text:
What it's for. Offering one of your own campuses as a mobility destination — to your other campuses, or to your partners.

Who it's for. admin

How it works. A switch, in the campus list you already maintain. You turn it on, and the campus becomes a destination.

Its record is created from what you have already entered — name, address, domain. There is no double entry, and nothing more to fill in to get started.

Your campuses can then exchange students with each other. A student from the Lyon campus sees the Toulouse one like any other destination — but not their own: their campus stays visible without being selectable.

Turning the switch off removes the campus from destinations. You can turn it back on: the record is kept, not rebuilt.

Your campuses, each with its switch. The one turned on carries the "Destination" badge: it has become a destination like any other.

Use case.

The school has three campuses. It opens all three, and its first-year students can spend a semester on another campus without leaving the same campaign process they would use for an international mobility.

docs.title: Onboarding incoming students
docs.text:
Onboarding is the stay of a student you host, from their first access to their transcript. It is steered with two objects:

  • a welcome path, which describes what the student has to do — built once under Settings ▸ Workflows;
  • a welcome session, which groups an intake of incoming students and names the path it applies.

The counterpart of a campaign, on the incoming side

What a campaign is to outgoing students, the welcome session is to incoming ones: it gathers a group, applies a path to it, and carries its tracking. Both screens read and work the same way.

docs.title: Opening a welcome session
docs.text:
What it is for. Keeping your intakes apart. Autumn and spring have neither the same dates nor necessarily the same requirements.

Who it is for. IO officer / coordinator

How it works. Under Onboarding, New session: you name the session — "Autumn 2026 intake" — and pick the path it applies. Only incoming paths are offered.

A session can be renamed, duplicated, and closed when the intake ends. Two sessions cannot carry the same name.

A session without a path asks for nothing

The path is what gives the student work to do. A session opened without one takes in files that have no step to clear. The screen says so and offers to plug one in.

docs.title: Accepting a nomination into a session
docs.text:
What it is for. Attaching every incoming student to their intake at the moment of acceptance, rather than later and forgetting.

How it works. When you accept a nomination, the screen always asks for the welcome session the student joins. The student then receives that session's path, and their onboarding file knows which session it was opened in.

A file already under way keeps its place: changing a session's path does not restart the steps already cleared.

Opening access

Access is opened from the session. It asks you to pick the session — without that choice, nothing is saved. The state of each access is read on the tracking: not sent yet, sent on such a date, or already signed in.

docs.title: Following where everyone stands
docs.text:
What it is for. Knowing at a glance who is waiting for what.

How it works. The session carries the same tracking as a campaign, with the same views and the same tools: table or kanban, search that suggests filters, sorting, card-line picker, saved views and Export what is on screen.

A session's table adds what only makes sense for an incoming student: their home institution, country, level, field of study and home city, alongside progress, current step and the state of their access.

docs.title: What the hosted student sees
docs.text:
How it works. The student finds their path on My onboarding: a single task list, in order, with what is asked of them at each step. Steps that mirror an act done elsewhere tick without them doing anything.

Documents in their file only open once validated: a transcript or a certificate still being produced is not shown half-made.

One document, one validation

A document uploaded by an incoming student is validated by their home institution, not twice. The host institution can open it and read it; it does not redo the validation work.

Use case.

The school hosts twenty-six incoming students in the autumn. It builds an eight-step path — proof of funds, language test, charter to accept, hosting certificate, campus choice, then courses — and opens the "Autumn 2026 intake" session. Every accepted nomination joins that session and receives the path. The coordinator filters the kanban on what is waiting for her: three files, and the rest moves on without her.

docs.title: Settings & team
docs.text: Settings bring together your institution's administrative configuration: its structure (campuses, organizational units, academic levels), team and permissions management, the user directory, personalised working views, and the connection to external systems. It is the control centre of the international relations office.

docs.title: Campuses
docs.text:
What it's for. Declare your institution's campuses (name, city, country, one main campus), to attach students to a campus and reflect your real structure.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. A management screen (Settings ▸ Institution) lists the campuses with the number of students attached to each. Deletion is blocked while students are still attached, to prevent any loss of link.

Your physical sites, with the number of students attached to each.

Use case.

A multi-site school declares its Paris and Lyon campuses, then assigns students to each.

docs.title: Organizational units (OUnits)
docs.text:
What it's for. Maintain your institution's EWP organizational units (faculties, departments), so Erasmus (EWP) data exchange references the correct sub-structures.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. A management screen lists the units, each with a name, an optional description and an identifier. It works like the campuses screen.

Use case.

The office declares the "Faculty of Engineering" as a unit with its EWP identifier.

docs.title: Custom academic levels
docs.text:
What it's for. Name your academic levels with your own vocabulary (for example "Aéro 4", "M1 Ingé") while keeping a standard mapping (EQF) behind the scenes — so dropdowns are familiar to your team and EWP exchange stays standards-compliant.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. A management screen (Settings ▸ Institution) lets you create, edit and delete your level labels, each mapped to an EQF level. Each row shows how many places or agreements use that level. Duplicate labels are rejected.

Your own level labels, each mapped to a European level and carrying its direction, with how many students, institutions and places depend on them.

Use case.

An engineering school defines "Aéro 4" mapped to EQF 7, to filter campaigns and agreements by its real level names.

docs.title: Mobility paths
docs.text:
What it's for. Building, under Settings ▸ Workflows, the list of what a student has to do during a mobility — for the students you send as well as the ones you host.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. This is the workshop: you build a path here, duplicate it, archive it. Plugging it in happens elsewhere — on a campaign or on a welcome session. Everything is detailed on the Mobility paths page, and a guide sits next to the workshop in the tool.

docs.title: Connectors: email, calendar, API
docs.text:
What it's for. Bringing together in one place the three ways of linking AroundLink to what you already use.

Who it's for. the whole mobility team, and your IT for the API

How it works. Settings ▸ Connectors carries three sections:

Connection What it does Email the Outlook add-in files your exchanges on the contact's fiche — see Emails & connectors Calendar your agenda read from Outlook, Google Calendar or Apple Calendar, read-only API your own systems read and write AroundLink data

The API key is personal, not your institution's

Each user has their own. Regenerating it leaves a colleague's working — and revokes yours only. It is a sensitive credential: never share it publicly, and regenerate it if you believe it may have been exposed.

Use case.

The school's IT team plugs its student registry into the API with the key of the developer who looks after it. When they leave the institution, that key is regenerated: the other integrations keep running.

docs.title: Protected deletions
docs.text:
What it's for. Stop you from deleting a setting still in use somewhere, and tell you exactly where it is used.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. Your campuses, periods, study levels, document types and tags each show a usage counter. As long as it is not at zero, deletion is refused and the detail tells you what depends on it — an agreement, a campaign, a student file.

You remain free to rename an item at any time: the change carries everywhere it appears, breaking nothing.

Use case.

The coordinator wants to delete a period that is no longer needed; the counter shows it is still used by three agreements, which they adjust before retrying.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
What it's for. Create your own labels to organise your students and partner institutions by your own criteria — a cohort, a programme, a group of destinations, a point to watch.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. Each tag carries a name and a colour, and applies to one of three scopes:

  • General — offered on both students and partners
  • Student — offered on students only
  • Institution — offered on partners only, and usable as a campaign filter

Once your tags exist, you apply them from the student or partner lists. Select several rows to add or remove tags across the whole selection at once.

Your tags, their scope and colour, with how many institutions and students each is applied to.

Use case.

The coordinator creates a "Double degree exchange" tag scoped to Institution, applies it to the twelve partners concerned, then uses it to narrow the destinations of a campaign.

Scope and campaign filters

A tag whose scope changes after it has been used in a campaign stops being taken into account there. Check your running campaigns before changing the scope of an existing tag.

docs.title: Student filters
docs.text:
What it's for. Describe your students with your own criteria — and, when you choose to, make those criteria visible to your students as they search for a destination.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A student filter carries a name and a colour, and applies to students or to institutions. You set it from a student's record, right beside their tags, and you find it again as a column in your lists: it sorts and filters like its neighbours.

The difference with a tag fits in one sentence: a tag stays with you, a student filter shows. Tick "Visible to students" and the value appears in "Find your exchange", where your students pick it like a country or a language. "Match my profile" then pre-selects the values a student already carries.

Your filters, their colour, and how many institutions and students each is applied to.

Use case.

The coordinator creates the "Double degree" filter, applies it to the students concerned and makes it visible. A student carrying it opens their destination search: the filter is already ticked, and they only see the destinations that concern them.

docs.title: Tag or student filter?
docs.text:
The two objects look alike — a name, a colour, applied to records — and that is exactly why they get confused. Yet they answer opposite questions.

Tag Student filter Who sees the value Your institution, and nobody else Your students too, as soon as you tick "Visible to students" What it is for Organising your work Helping the student recognise themselves and choose Where it appears Your lists, your campaign filters Your lists and the student's destination search "Match my profile" No effect Pre-selects the values the student carries Possible scopes General, Student, Institution Students, Institutions

Student filters applied to a selection of institutions — these are what your students will find in their search.

Tags, in the same place and on the same selection — but these never leave your institution.

The deciding question is a single one: who needs to see this value?

An internal point to watch, a note for the team, an administrative follow-up, something that belongs to you alone: that is a tag. A characteristic the student recognises as their own and will pick a destination on: that is a student filter.

The word \"tag\" never appears on this screen

That is deliberate. Mixing the two vocabularies is exactly what leads to putting internal information where students will read it.

docs.title: Saved views
docs.text:
What it's for. Save a table configuration (chosen columns, widths, filters, sort order) on a given page, then reapply it in one click. Each coordinator instantly recovers their working layout without rebuilding it every time.

Who it's for. RI manager

How it works. On a table page, you adjust the columns, filters and sort, then save that layout as a view. You can then switch between your views in one click. Views are private to your institution.

Your periods, each with its direction and its rank in the year — "the 1st of 2". The banner at the top flags those still to classify: without that rank, your nominations cannot be exported to the EWP Dashboard.

Use case.

A coordinator saves a "Spain partners — active agreements" view with its columns and filters, and reopens it in one click each session.

docs.title: Team & invitations
docs.text:
What it's for. Manage your office's members: prepare their accounts ahead of time, then open access at the right moment. Ideal for a grouped start on launch day.

Who it's for. admin

How it works. You create the team's accounts in a "pending" state, with no email sent. When ready, you open access individually or for all pending accounts at once: each member then receives their invitation. Sends are error-tolerant — a single failure does not interrupt the whole batch.

Use case.

During setup, the admin prepares 8 accounts (pending), then clicks "Send all access" on launch day.

docs.title: What your students see
docs.text:
What it's for. Setting two sensitive pieces of information your students see — or do not — without changing anything for your team.

Who it's for. admin

How it works. Two switches, independent of each other.

Ranking. By default a student sees their rank within their promotion on their own profile. You can hide it from them: you and your team still see it, they do not.

Number of places. By default your students see how many places you open on each partner and period. You can show only that a place is available, without the number.

The two switches, each with the sentence saying what the student will see.

Use case.

The institution would rather the ranking did not circulate among students before the committee meets. The admin hides it for the duration of the campaign and restores it afterwards — the coordinators saw it throughout.

docs.title: Roles & permissions
docs.text:
What it's for. Defining who can do what, and to whom — fitting access to your organisation rather than to an imposed split.

Who it's for. admin

How it works. A role is built in two steps.

First its perimeter, meaning what it covers. Four questions, in this order: the business domains concerned, the direction (outgoing only, incoming only, or both), the campuses, the promotions. The lists offered are your own settings, never a generic list. Ticking nothing on campuses or promotions means "all of them".

The domain comes first because it prunes what follows: setting rights and then finding half of them gone would be work thrown away.

Then its rights, line by line, with four levels:

Level What it allows None Nothing. Set on a category, it closes everything inside it. View Consult and search. No change leaves the tool. Prepare Create, edit, upload — the file moves forward, inside. Decide Validate, refuse, send, delete, export — it leaves the tool.

The useful boundary is this one: "Prepare" moves a file forward inside your walls, "Decide" sends it out. The four levels sit side by side on each line, with no dropdown: seeing the neighbouring value is part of the information.

One line of rights: the four levels aligned, the one in force in colour, and the arrow that hands the line back to what it inherits.

The perimeter step: business domains, direction, campuses and promotions. Ticking nothing on campuses or promotions covers them all.

The full tree: each section of the application, and under it the actions a role can carry.

Comparing two roles. A button shows the same tree with one column per role. That is how you answer "who can actually approve a grant?" without opening roles one by one — and how you find out in time that nobody can, because everyone assumed someone else did.

The same tree, one column per role: you read at a glance who decides, who prepares and who sees nothing.

A safety net. You cannot remove your institution's last administrator.

What others see. When a right is missing, the screen says so instead of pretending: a banner announces read-only mode, and a note explains that a student is outside your perimeter.

Use case.

The manager creates an "Incoming officer" role: perimeter limited to incoming students and the Lyon campus, "Decide" on documents, "View" on agreements, "None" on grants.

docs.title: My permissions
docs.text:
What it's for. Seeing for yourself what you are allowed to do, and to whom.

Who it's for. any team member

How it works. The screen states your rights in plain words and recalls your perimeter.

It is behind no permission of its own, and that is deliberate: the more restricted a role, the more the person needs to understand why a screen is closed to them. Without it, every restriction looks like a breakdown, and someone else has to go and read their configuration for them.

Your rights stated as sentences — whose files you see, and what you can do in each section.

docs.title: A contact's record
docs.text:
What it's for. Bringing together on one screen everything you know about a contact, whether they are a person in your directory, a member of your team, or both.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A directory contact and a login account used to be two separate records with no link between them. It is now one contact, one page: your contact grids and your team list lead to the same place, and you see both their details and the state of their access.

docs.title: User directory
docs.text:
What it's for. A read-only overview of all the users linked to your institution — students, team members and invited partner users — filterable by type, status and free-text search.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. A page gathers all the organisation's users and lets you filter them by category, status or name/email. It is reserved for paid mobility plans.

An import: the template to download, the required columns, and the row-by-row preview before you confirm.

Use case.

The admin searches a user by email to check their status and category.

docs.title: Mobility paths
docs.text:
A path — a workflow in the interface — is the list of things a student has to do during a mobility. You build it once, then apply it to a group of students: each of them moves at their own pace, and you see where everyone stands.

It replaces the old onboarding sequence: one workshop now serves the students you send and the students you host.

Where it happens

Settings ▸ Workflows to build a path. You plug it in elsewhere: on a campaign for outgoing students, on a welcome session for incoming ones. A path that is plugged in nowhere does nothing.

docs.title: One path per direction
docs.text:
What it is for. Sending and hosting do not call for the same pieces. The direction is chosen when you create the path and never changes: it decides where the path can be used.

Who it is for. IO officer / coordinator

How it works.

Direction For whom What usually goes in Outgoing the students you send from the partner's yes to the return: identity document, insurance, learning agreement, arrival and departure certificates, transcript Incoming the students you host from arrival to transcript: information check, documents, charter, campus and course choice, feedback

Two mechanics only exist in one direction, and the screen says so before you find out by having the step refused:

  • Choose campus only exists for incoming students — the host institution is the one with several sites;
  • Choose courses too — it reads the host's course catalogue and feeds the incoming transcript. For a student you send, the equivalent is the learning agreement, which lives in its own module.

Start from an existing path

The copy icon on each row duplicates a path under a new name. It beats the blank page, and two close paths stay comparable.

docs.title: Plugging the path in
docs.text:
What it is for. A path on its own starts nothing. It begins when you attach it to a group.

How it works.

  • Outgoing — open a campaign, Edit, settings tab, Mobility workflow field. Every student accepted by a partner then receives the path automatically. The field is optional: you can plug it in later from the campaign's Mobility tab.
  • Incoming — under Onboarding, create a welcome session, name it, pick its path. When you accept a nomination, you choose which session the student joins.

The same path can serve several campaigns or sessions. The Used by column in the list tells you how many.

Changing a step reaches those already on their way

A path in service is not frozen: a change to a step reaches every student already following it. Check the Used by column before touching a step, and the Students column to know how many files are concerned.

Changing a campaign's path asks for confirmation

The replacement happens from the screen it governs, and asks for confirmation: students already under way switch to the new path.

docs.title: What a step can ask for
docs.text:
What it is for. Each step carries one action type, which decides who acts and what moves the student on.

How it works. The catalogue is closed, by design: each type plugs into a function that already exists in the tool — a document type, a template, the course catalogue, the validation queue. A step is therefore never a free-text field: the path orders existing functions and makes them compulsory at the right moment.

Step type Available for Who acts What moves the student on Complete profile both directions the student they have filled in the fields you picked, checked the rest, and confirmed their information is correct Deposit documents both directions the student every requested document is uploaded Request a language test both directions the student the test you asked for is provided, certificate and scores Generate a document both directions nobody — automatic the platform produces the document; the student confirms they have read and downloaded it Generate, then collect signed both directions the student they return, signed, the document the platform issued Choose campus incoming only the student they have picked one of your campuses Read and accept both directions the student they tick that they have read and accepted — the wording accepted is kept as it was on that day Choose courses incoming only the student they have handed in their course selection Give feedback both directions the student they write their review, you moderate it in the validation queue: accepted on every topic asked closes the step, refused sends it back for a rewrite Mirror something done elsewhere both directions nobody — a mirror see below

A language test is not a document like any other

You list the tests you accept — IELTS, TOEFL iBT, Duolingo — and one of them is enough. What is expected is not only a scanned PDF, but the structured result: test type, overall score, the four skills, the European level. That is what lets you decide.

The target date blocks nothing

Each step can carry an indicative date. It guides the student, nothing more: handing in later does not block the step. Leave it empty if you do not want one.

docs.title: Steps that tick themselves
docs.text:
What it is for. Most steps in a path are not things anyone does inside the path. They watch an object that already exists elsewhere in AroundLink — a signed learning agreement, a validated document, a grant payment — and tick on their own when it changes. They untick too, if the object goes back.

How it works. That is why you cannot tick them by hand, and why they are not in the type list when you add a step: the platform sets them up, with the object they watch. The paths delivered with AroundLink already contain them — "learning agreement signed by all three", "confirmation of arrival", "transcript validated".

A mirror copies nothing

The step does not duplicate the data: it reads the original object. There are therefore never two versions of the same fact, and a withdrawn signature sends the step back to pending.

docs.title: Ordering, folding, archiving
docs.text:
How it works. Steps are reordered by dragging them from one card to another, and each step declares the phase it belongs to — before, during or after the mobility. It is that phase which feeds mobility tracking.

The path list sorts and filters. Its State column speaks: With steps, With students, Not in use, Inactive. A path you no longer want goes to the archives — Archive, then View archived workflows to find it again and restore it.

Use case.

The school builds two paths: an outgoing one in nine steps, an incoming one in seven. The outgoing path is plugged into this year's campaign; the incoming one into the "Autumn 2026 intake" session. The four learning-agreement and transcript steps are mirrors: nobody ticks them, they follow the documents. The coordinator therefore only watches the five steps that really ask for something.

docs.title: Partners & institution files
docs.text: The Partners module brings together, in one place, every institution your international relations office works with: where they are, what agreements bind you, how many places remain open, and the state of their official data. Each partner has a complete file that your students and your team consult throughout the year.

docs.title: Partner directory
docs.text:
What it's for. A single, filterable table of all your partner institutions. It gives an immediate overview — country, city, accreditations, tags, languages, levels, remaining places, number and type of agreements — and acts as the entry point into each partner file.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The directory lists the partners your institution tracks (those you have an agreement with or that you created). You filter the list straight from the search bar, then click a row to open the file. A toggle switches the same table to the consolidated agreements view.

Your partners, with their internal code, accreditations, your tags and the levels open. Click the image to enlarge it.

Use case.

A coordinator filters on "Spain + active agreements", then opens a university's file to check its contacts.

docs.title: Create a partner institution
docs.text:
What it's for. Register a new partner not yet on the platform, capturing its identity, location, official identifiers and at least one main contact. The partner immediately becomes visible in the directory and available for agreements.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The form starts with the institution's domain — the one its professional email addresses use. That is what identifies an institution reliably, where two similar names often mean the same school.

Before creating anything, the platform checks that domain and shows you the records it already knows. Three outcomes:

  • That's the one — you attach the existing record to your directory. No duplicate is created, and you inherit what is already filled in.
  • None of these is my partner — your request goes to our team, who complete the shared reference.
  • It is unknown — you create it, with at least one main contact.

On save, the partner is attached to your institution and its contacts are linked to any matching existing accounts. You are then redirected to the full file to keep editing.

Beyond the domain, only the name is required: the rest is filled in as you learn it.

Use case.

The office signs a new partner in Portugal; the coordinator adds it with its Erasmus code and the receiving coordinator as main contact.

docs.title: Institution file (Information)
docs.text:
What it's for. The editable identity card of a partner: description, accreditations, links, private tags, internal code, logo and photo. Everything the office wants to remember about a partner is centralised here.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. One page combines the information form, logo and photo uploads, and the expected language-scores block. Descriptive fields are editable; the official technical identifiers stay read-only. Saving only affects your own tags and your internal code for that partner; other institutions' data on a shared partner is never modified.

A partner's fiche: on the left their identity card, which stays on screen — including your tags and student filters; in the middle the index of sections with what is left to fill in; on the right what you keep to yourself. At the bottom, their agenda and the button that asks them for their dates.

Use case.

The coordinator tags Bologna as "Priority" and records the office's internal reference for that institution.

docs.title: Partner tags
docs.text:
What it's for. Define your own colour-coded labels (for example "Priority", "Double degree", "Watch") and apply them to partners for grouping and filtering. Tags are private to the institution that creates them.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. A management screen (Settings ▸ Institution) lets you create, edit and delete tags, each with a name and a colour. Tags are applied from the partner file and appear as badges and filters in the directory.

Use case.

The office creates a red "Suspended" tag and applies it to two partners whose agreements have expired.

docs.title: Partner internal code
docs.text:
What it's for. Record your own internal identifier for each partner, distinct from the official code, to map partners onto your existing spreadsheets or management tools.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. It's not a separate screen: just a field on the partner file. Left blank, it clears the code; filled in, it creates or updates a reference private to your institution. It appears as a column in the directory.

Use case.

The coordinator records the internal reference "IT-BOL-01" for Bologna.

docs.title: Expected language scores
docs.text:
What it's for. Record the language-test thresholds a partner expects from incoming students (for example IELTS 6.5, TOEFL 90, B2), on the same scale students declare — so the two can be compared directly during selection.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A management block (add, edit, delete via a dialog) on the partner file. Each entry reuses the student-score structure: test type, overall score, the four sub-scores and an optional CEFR level. The test reference now states which language each test measures, so a requirement and a certificate can be matched without interpretation.

Requiring two languages. A requirement is no longer a flat list of alternatives. The screen stacks numbered requirements, each carrying its language, and you join two of them with one click on the word that separates them:

The separator says What the student must do and satisfy both — "English and German" or satisfy either one

Inside a requirement, the tests listed are always alternatives: the header says so — any one of these is enough when there are several, this proof is required when there is only one.

This is what finally expresses what a university really asks when it requires a second language on top of English: before, the student stayed eligible as soon as English was satisfied.

The grade point average holds its own requirement apart — the screen marks it Not a language: it is a prerequisite, not a language.

Where a requirement comes from. The same fiche can carry two origins, and the difference matters — one applies to everyone, the other to you alone. A note at the top of the block says which:

Note What it means Published by this partner the partner publishes its own requirement from its own fiche; it applies to all its clients Provided by this partner the fiche is kept by the partner: you view, you do not change Only your institution sees this this is your record for this partner — ring-fenced, nobody else sees it

When the partner publishes its requirement, that one decides: your line stays visible but no longer applies, and the counter only counts what acts. You can take it back at home — your value applies again, for your institution only.

A source column gives the same information row by row, and the fiche says who filled it in.

What your institution publishes

The counterpart, seen from your side: the scores you require of your incoming students are entered under My institution, and your partners read them on your fiche. An institution on a free plan publishes its language requirements — and nothing else.

Use case.

The coordinator records "Lund: IELTS 6.5 / B2"; a student at IELTS 6.0 is then flagged below the threshold. Six months later Lund publishes its own requirement at 7.0: it takes over, and the coordinator's line stays visible but marked as no longer applying.

docs.title: A partner's cities
docs.text:
What it's for. Many partners have several sites — Berlin, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt. Those cities only lived in a free-text field: you could not send a student there, nor put places on them.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. You declare a partner's cities yourself from its fiche: a name, a country. They appear under its name, collapsible, and the institution itself counts among its places — at the top, labelled Main.

A switch on each city turns it on as a destination: it then becomes a full campaign destination that a student can wish for, and the student sees it like any other destination.

These cities are ring-fenced

The cities you declare for a partner belong to you alone. Another institution working with the same partner does not see them. The padlock on the list says so.

A partner who keeps its own fiche keeps control

If the partner manages its own campuses, those are the ones that count: you view them, you do not add on top. Two sets of cities for a single institution would make no sense. And a city does not contain cities — the screen does not offer it.

Places follow the place. A place belongs to its agreement and carries the location it is meant for: the cities' matrices stack up in the places page, each announcing what it already carries. Three campuses therefore do not add three agreements.

Switch off before deleting

A city turned on as a destination cannot be deleted: students may already have chosen it, and its places would go with it. Switch it off first — the screen says so and refuses clearly. The deletion is then confirmed, and it is definitive.

docs.title: Partner contacts
docs.text:
What it's for. A directory of the people the office deals with at each partner, one designated as main. These contacts feed the agreement and signatory dropdowns.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. Two entry points: a global list of your contacts and a "Relationship" tab per partner. Each contact has name, email, phone, position and a "main" flag. On save, a contact is automatically linked to a matching existing account.

Your contacts at partner institutions, the "Main" badge marking the one who receives requests and nominations. This is where you open their access.

Use case.

The coordinator adds a partner's Erasmus officer and marks them as the main contact.

docs.title: Open portal access (invitations)
docs.text:
What it's for. Open partner-side access for a contact so they collaborate directly (for example to approve an agreement). In one click, the system invites the contact, links them to an existing account, or reports a conflict.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. From a partner contact, "Open access" sends an email invitation; a "Resend" action re-issues it. Both are rate-limited to avoid repeated sends.

Use case.

The coordinator invites the partner's Erasmus officer so she can review an agreement in her own portal.

docs.title: Consolidated agreements view
docs.text:
What it's for. A unified view merging Erasmus (IIA) and bilateral agreements across all your partners, to see and filter in one place each agreement's status, validity years, signing date and approval state.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A toggle switches the directory to this normalised view, one row per agreement. Each row shows the partner, the source (IIA or bilateral), the type, the status (active / inactive / terminated), local and partner approval, and the validity years.

Use case.

The office filters "All agreements" on "Expired" to plan renewals.

docs.title: Institution lookup (autocomplete)
docs.text:
What it's for. Speed up data entry by suggesting known institutions as you type, to attach partners and agreements to the right, correctly-named institution.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A field suggests the institutions matching your input; autocomplete is built into the relevant forms.

Use case.

Typing "sorbon" suggests "Sorbonne Université" with its identifiers.

docs.title: Partner student content
docs.text:
What it's for. Compose the practical information students see about a partner (description and content blocks grouped by category), to give consistent guidance approved by the office.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. An editor with a description field and the add, edit or delete of content blocks grouped by sub-category. A bulk import can also load this content from a file.

Use case.

The office fills in the "Housing" and "Visa" blocks of a partner so they appear on its student page.

docs.title: Partner document library
docs.text:
What it's for. Keep the files attached to a partner (signed agreements, brochures…), to gather all partner documents in one place.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. You upload named documents to a partner (duplicate names are rejected), list them, and delete them individually.

The documents you publish to your students about this partner.

Use case.

The coordinator uploads the signed cooperation-agreement PDF to the partner file.

docs.title: Partner course catalogue
docs.text:
What it's for. Maintain the list of courses available at a partner for the exchange, so students and the office know what can be studied there.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. You add courses via a form and delete them per partner; they are listed by code.

Each course now declares where and when it is taught, and to whom:

  • the campuses it is taught on — a campus page only shows its own;
  • the incoming periods it is open to;
  • the incoming promotions that can take it.

Two columns summarise this in the list: Open to — the promotions — and Available in — the periods. The catalogue can then be filtered by period.

A label is incoming OR outgoing, never both

Your mobility periods and your custom academic levels now carry a direction. Everything that existed was switched to outgoing. A consequence worth knowing: levels and periods only appear on your pages once your incoming labels are declared. If a page looks empty on that side, that is where to look.

The course catalogue — here your own institution's. Each course says which campuses it is taught on and in which term. The "Open to" and "Available in" columns appear as well once you have declared your incoming labels.

docs.title: Importing a catalogue instead of typing it
docs.text:
What it's for. A catalogue is typed course by course when it is new. But when you start from learning agreements signed years ago, typing is not viable — and that is precisely where the material most useful to your students sits.

How it works. Settings ▸ Integrations ▸ Import Courses, in three steps: you download the template, you upload your file to preview every row and fix errors inline, then you confirm — only valid rows are written. Excel or CSV.

Each row needs the course name and one way to name the partner: your own internal code, its domain, or its ROR id — checked in that order.

The screen states what it requires before you even open the file: the mandatory columns, the eight columns it accepts, and the formats.

The template is deliberately tolerant

Credits and the ISCED code are optional: an agreement signed five years ago almost never carries them. Refusing those rows would mean throwing away most of the file for a value nobody will ever recover.

However, a row must carry at least one of the three identifiers — otherwise it is refused: we would not know which partner it is about.

A column the template does not list is simply ignored: you can keep your own notes in the file. But a renamed column is read as a missing one.

Re-importing updates, it does not duplicate

The same file passed a second time updates the courses instead of creating doubles. You can therefore fix your file and pass it again without any cleaning up.

A course without credits is not a zero-credit course

The screen shows a dash, not a zero, and the value stays empty rather than wrong. Such a course still travels through the learning agreement, the transcript and the totals — it blocks nothing there, it simply counts no credits.

Use case.

The office records the 12 English-taught master's courses a partner offers to incoming students. For the 270 agreements of previous years, it imports the file: courses with no ISCED go through, rows with no identifier at all are flagged.

docs.title: Partner FAQ
docs.text:
What it's for. Gathering the questions your students always ask about a destination, and their answers.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. What you see depends on the nature of the partner, on the same principle as its factsheet, course catalogue and library:

  • The partner is itself an AroundLink client — it publishes its own FAQ, which you read as written, marked "Provided by this partner". It updates when they change it; you have nothing to maintain.
  • The partner is not a client — it broadcasts nothing, so the FAQ is yours. You write it about them, for your students, and your institution alone sees it.

Each question carries its category and the audience it addresses.

Use case.

The same three questions came up every year about housing in Lisbon. The coordinator writes them once in the record's FAQ; their students now find them before writing in.

docs.title: Partner web & social links
docs.text:
What it's for. Record a partner's website and social networks, so students and staff can reach its official channels.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A form edits the website, Instagram, LinkedIn, Twitter and Facebook, with a save confirmation and a clear flag when something is wrong.

Use case.

The coordinator adds a partner's Instagram so it appears on the student page.

docs.title: Student-feedback moderation
docs.text:
What it's for. Review, accept (and publish) or refuse the feedback your students leave about their host institution, controlling what future students see while keeping a record of each decision.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. A view by status (pending / accepted / refused) with counters. Accepting can publish the review (visible to students) or keep it hidden; refusing hides it and records a reason. Each decision writes a history entry with the author. Reviews appear in two places: on the partner's page, and in a dedicated tab on the profile of the student who wrote them.

What you see. Only the reviews written by your students. A review written by another institution's student — even about a partner you also track — is never shown to you, whatever its status.

Use case.

A coordinator reads a pending review, publishes the positive ones and refuses an inappropriate one with a reason.

Paid plan only

Reading and moderating reviews are part of the paid plan. An institution on free access does not have this screen.

docs.title: Preview as student
docs.text:
What it's for. Show the office exactly what a student sees on a partner's page — places by category, level and field, requirements, published reviews — to verify the file before students rely on it.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The preview displays the partner's student page, with place distributions gathered across all agreement types, filterable by year, level and field. With no student profile, filters start on "All".

Use case.

Before a campaign opens, the coordinator previews a partner to confirm the display of places and requirements.

docs.title: Hide, archive or merge a partner
docs.text:
What it's for. Take a partner you no longer work with out of circulation, or bring together two records pointing at the same institution, without ever losing the history of past mobilities.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. Three moves, from the lightest to the most final. Hiding removes the partner from your students' view while keeping it in your internal lists. Archiving also takes it out of your campaigns and destination counts. Merging brings two records into one: the agreements, contacts and mobilities of the absorbed record are attached to the one you keep.

In all three cases, nothing is deleted. Mobilities already completed with that partner remain visible in the files of the students concerned.

Use case.

After a university merger, the coordinator brings the two records into one; the agreements from both end up in the same place, with no re-entry.

Contact access

Archiving a partner revokes the access you had opened for its contacts. They can no longer sign in until the partner is reactivated.

docs.title: Import partner institutions
docs.text:
What it's for. Bulk-load or refresh many partners from an Excel file, with strict header checking so a badly-filled template doesn't silently import zero rows.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. You upload the file; headers are checked up front (missing or unknown columns flagged); rows are imported and a failing row is skipped without blocking the others. Re-importing an existing institution refreshes its filled-in fields. A summary reports creations, updates and skipped rows.

Use case.

The office uploads 300 partners: 280 created, 20 updated, a header typo caught before any save.

docs.title: Import partner contacts
docs.text:
What it's for. Bulk-load partner contacts from a CSV or Excel file, matching them to partners by email domain, with a preview before writing.

Who it's for. RI manager / admin

How it works. You upload the file, a preview is shown without writing anything, then you confirm. A failing row is skipped, the others continue. The summary reports creations, updates, skipped rows and email domains matching no known partner.

Use case.

The office uploads a contact list: each one joins the right partner, and 3 unknown domains are flagged.

docs.title: Mobility tracking
docs.text:
Once the path is plugged in, tracking answers the only question you ask when you open a file: where does this student stand, and do I have anything to do?

The same tracking serves both directions — the students you send and the ones you host — with the same words, the same views and the same filters.

docs.title: The three phases of a mobility
docs.text:
What it is for. Sorting files in the order of time rather than in the order of steps. You do not steer someone who has not left the way you steer someone who is back.

Who it is for. the whole mobility team

How it works. Each step of a path declares its phase, and a file's phase is the first one that is not finished. It is therefore not declarative: it follows from the work actually done.

Phase Read on a file What it covers Before the mobility Not departed everything before departure: documents, learning agreement, insurance During the mobility On site the stay: arrival confirmed, courses, on-site follow-up After the mobility Returned the return: departure certificate, transcript, feedback Closed Closed the file is closed

A phase follows, it is not typed in

You do not move a student from one phase to another by hand. Move the steps on — or let the mirrors tick — and the phase follows. A finished file says so even without a closing date.

docs.title: Two views of the same tracking
docs.text:
What it is for. The table to work through, the kanban to see what is coming.

How it works. Both views share the same toolbar: search, sorting, filters, column picker, saved views and export.

The table lines the files up in rows, with progress in figures, the current step and who is expected. Eight optional columns can be added and sorted: Destination, City, Country, Region, Period, Level, Field of study, Agreement, Workflow.

The kanban gives one column per phase and one card per student. Each column scrolls inside itself, its title stays visible, and the gauge at the top says how many files have passed the step — mirrors included. You pick up to thirteen facts to show on the cards, and the whole card leads to the file.

The kanban's search suggests filters as you type: Destination, City, Country, Region, Period, Level, Field of study, Agreement, Phase.

The export takes what you have in front of you

The Export what is on screen button takes your filters, your visible columns and your sorting. It is available on both views and in both directions.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
How it works. Tracking appears in four places, and it is always the same screen:

  • a campaign's Mobility tab — every outgoing student of that campaign. If no path is plugged in, the tab says what is missing and offers to plug it in on the spot;
  • a welcome session — every incoming student of that session;
  • a student's Mobility tab — one block per mobility: a student who left twice has two files, each with its dates and its progress;
  • the dashboard, which gives the summary by phase.

A mobility header always reads the same way: where, what, when — the partner with its logo, the agreement family, the period. And the breadcrumb goes all the way down to the open session.

docs.title: The mobility timeline
docs.text:
What it is for. Reading a mobility in time rather than as a list: from the first wish to the closing.

How it works. The timeline carries real dates and distinguishes its two sources — what comes from the campaign and what comes from the path. It does not go back in time, and the current day does not count as past. Campaign dates appear even if the student has submitted no wish.

It is also what a student's agenda shows: the dated timeline of their mobility, sorted into overdue, upcoming and past.

docs.title: Who is expected
docs.text:
How it works. On every row and every card, Waiting on says who holds the ball: the student, you, or nobody when the step is a mirror. A step that nothing blocks is due, not pending — the distinction saves you looking for a blockage that does not exist.

Shortcuts lead straight to the object named: a student's name opens their fiche, a path's name opens its workshop, a transcript's badge opens the entry screen.

Use case.

At the end of September, the coordinator opens the campaign's Mobility tab. The kanban shows four files still Not departed although classes have started. She filters on Waiting on: you, finds three learning agreements waiting for her signature, handles them, and the three cards move to On site on their own.

docs.title: Validations
docs.text: Everything waiting for a decision from you, in one place: documents uploaded by your students, learning agreements to sign, transcripts to issue. It is the screen you open in the morning to see what is blocked.

docs.title: Validation Hub
docs.text:
What it does. A single queue where the coordinator validates everything the student submits during their mobility — administrative files, learning agreements, transcripts and testimonials about partners — without having to browse several screens. Items that have been waiting a long time are flagged as urgent, and every decision is archived with its author, its outcome and the refusal reason.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The queue gathers pending documents, OLAs awaiting the institution's signature, transcripts and testimonials, with counters (pending / students concerned / urgent). The coordinator opens each item and decides to validate or refuse; a comment is required when refusing. A "History" tab lists past decisions with their reason.

Everything waiting on your decision, with the number of overdue items and filters by document type.

Use case.

Monday morning, the coordinator sees 12 pending items, 3 of them urgent: they validate two passports, sign one OLA on behalf of the sending institution, and refuse an unreadable insurance certificate with a comment — all from the same queue.

docs.title: Students' administrative files
docs.text:
What it does. A central page listing all files uploaded by students (passport, insurance, language tests, arrival/departure certificates, etc.) with their status. The office validates or refuses files one by one or in bulk, records arrival dates and launches reminder campaigns to students whose documents are missing or were refused.

Who it's for. RI manager / coordinator

How it works. The coordinator filters the file list, validates or refuses several at once, enters a student's arrival date, estimates how many students would be reminded, then triggers a reminder campaign in one click.

Use case.

The coordinator filters on "Refused", selects 8 files, refuses them in bulk with a comment, then sends a reminder to the students concerned.

docs.title: Student portal — Discover & apply
docs.text: The student portal supports every student from their first login through to submitting their application. It brings together a journey dashboard, profile management, a partner-university search engine and the entire campaign wish-list flow. The goal: give students a clear, self-service experience while lightening the international office's workload.

docs.title: Mobility dashboard
docs.text:
What it's for. This is the student's home page. It shows where they stand in their whole mobility journey as a visual timeline, and highlights the next action to take. Students keep an overview without needing to understand the administrative machinery.

Who it's for. student

How it works. On each login, the portal automatically determines the student's status and displays it on an eleven-step timeline, from "Connected" to "Mobility completed". Each step passed is marked as completed, the current step is highlighted and links straight to the right page. Before any placement, the dashboard suggests a few partner universities to explore; once the student is placed, it shows the confirmed host university and a checklist of mobility steps.

The dashboard: their mobility timeline step by step, their confirmed destination and the list of actions still to complete.

Use case.

A student who has just submitted their wishes logs in and sees the "Application in progress" step highlighted, with a direct link to the campaign.

docs.title: Profile — Personal information
docs.text:
What it's for. Students manage their identity and academic details here, reused throughout the mobility process: name, contacts, emergency number, nationality, birth information, student number, academic level, campus and field of study. They also manage their profile photo here.

Who it's for. student

How it works. The student fills in a profile form and can upload a photo (PNG or JPG). The academic-level field adapts to the institution: if it has configured its own programmes (for example "Aéro 4"), those are shown; otherwise a generic level is offered. The field of study is based on the ISCED classification.

Use case.
